speakeroldname: Hon. Milton F. Gregg (Minister of Labour):
subtopic: REPORTED QUESTION OF VALIDITY OF FEDERAL LABOUR CODE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mrs. Fairclough) asked a question to which I will now reply. I assume the question refers to the reference made by the governor general in council to the Supreme Court of Canada under the provisions of the Supreme Court Act of certain questions of law relating to the application and validity of the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act. This reference has been set down by the supreme court for hearing during the current week and I understand the hearing is being proceeded with at this time.
Hon. members are probably aware that disputes arising in connection with the employment of longshoremen and stevedores in the loading and unloading of ships have been handled by my department under the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act since its inception, and prior to that for many years under the earlier Industrial Disputes Investigation Act.
However, in 1954, upon an application made by district No. 50 of the united mine workers to the Ontario labour relations board under the provision of the Ontario labour relations act, that board accepted jurisdiction and certified the applicant union as bargaining agent for employees of the Eastern Canada Stevedoring Company employed in the loading and unloading of ships at the docks in Toronto harbour.
The validity of this order of the Ontario board was challenged by a rival union which had theretofore exercised bargaining rights 50433-40J
for these employees, namely the brotherhood of railway and steamship clerks, freight handlers, express and station employees.
The attorney general of Ontario intervened in these proceedings and gave notice to the Attorney General of Canada that in the proceedings the constitutional validity of the federal statute, the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act, would be brought into question by the province on the ground that the act is ultra vires to the parliament of Canada because it is legislation in relation to property and civil rights in the province.
Since the validity of the federal legislation was thus raised in the proceedings, it was considered advisable by the government to have the application of the federal legislation in respect to the employees settled with the least possible delay by reference to the Supreme Court of Canada, and at the same time to obtain the opinion of the supreme court on the question raised by the attorney general of Ontario, namely the jurisdiction of parliament to enact the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act. The following questions of law have therefore been submitted to the Supreme Court of Canada for hearing and consideration, namely:
(1)	Does the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act, Revised Statutes of Canada, 1952, chapter 152, apply in respect of the employees in Toronto of the Eastern Canada Stevedoring Company Limited employed in connection with the loading and unloading of ships?
(2)	Is the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act ultra vires to the parliament of Canada, either in whole or in part and, if so, in what particular or particulars and to what extent?
Decision on the matter of amendments to the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act will be deferred pending receipt of the report of the supreme court on this reference.
With regard to the second part of my hon. friend's question, hon. members will also be aware that the railway unions representing non-operating employees of the railways have indicated that it is their intention to undertake an early study of the provisions of the Industrial Relations and Disputes Investigation Act relating to conciliation and to thereafter make

Inquiries of the Ministry appropriate representations to the government. Naturally, we would want to have the benefit of such representations and to have the opportunity of studying them when they are forthcoming. Consequently, for this reason also, we are postponing any further amendment to the act for the time being.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Monday last the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings (Mr. Nowlan) asked me if I could give any further information beyond what had appeared
Inquiries of the Ministry in the press with respect to a number of cases of methyl alcohol poisoning, which had occurred on H.M.C.S. Magnificent. I replied that as a board of inquiry was sitting to establish the facts, I felt that I should not make any further statement until it had completed its task.
The board of inquiry has now completed its investigation and is forwarding its findings to naval headquarters. While the report is, of course, a confidential report for the guidance of the naval authorities in taking whatever action may be warranted, I can give the house briefly the facts as to what took place.
Briefly the facts are that three cans of duplicating fluid, used in the ship's communication duplicating machines, were removed from a locked storeroom by a member of the ship's company, who had access to the key in the course of his normal duties. One can was removed during the early afternoon of Friday, January 21, and two further cans in the early evening of the same day. These cans were kept hidden and were passed around to several groups of seamen who surreptitiously drank the liquid mixed with soft drinks or grapefruit juice from cups and soft drink bottles. The cans, incidentally, were clearly and distinctly marked "poison" and bore other words of caution. When emptied they were thrown overboard during the night. There was no large party at any time during the day or night, but as I have mentioned, small groups of two to five men drank the mixture in widely separated places throughout the ship. There was no outward evidence of drunkenness on board during the time in question. There was no indication, therefore, to the officers making rounds that anything was amiss. The first evidence that anything was wrong was the sudden severe illness of a number of men. It is evident, I might add, that a great number of the men did not know what they had been drinking.
Great credit should be given to the ship's duty medical officer and to the staff of the Royal Canadian naval hospital at Halifax, as well as to civilian consultants, for the fact that due to their combined and prompt action the nature of the poisoning was quickly diagnosed and suitable treatment applied. Had this not been so, the consequences to the men involved would have been much more severe and in several cases would probably have proven fatal.
Following study of the report of the board of inquiry at naval headquarters, disciplinary action will be taken where appropriate, as well as such other steps as may appear desirable to prevent a recurrence of this regrettable incident.

In view of the general desire to save time and expedite the work of the session, Mr. Speaker, I shall forgo the usual compliments and make my remarks as short as possible. I am glad to see that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) is so sharp in his arithmetic today. He is much sharper than he was when he was speaking in this debate some two weeks ago. At that time his figures did not work out nearly as neatly as they did in his reply today.
I believe the earlier speech delivered by the minister calls for some comment. He took up nearly two full pages of Hansard, and I am told that means approximately 2,000 words, explaining the continuation in office of Dr. Thomson, head of the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act, during the time he was running for the position of leader of the Liberal party in Saskatchewan. Most of this so-called explanation was taken up with a long discussion of Dr. Thomson's suitability for this post. This is a question which, to my knowledge, no one has ever raised. In other words, the minister was raising a straw man and knocking him down. Throughout this lengthy explanation there was no mention of the real point at issue, the real reason for raising this matter here. The minister passed it over as though it did not exist.
The main point is very simple, Mr. Speaker. It concerns the propriety of a civil servant running for political office before he has ceased to be a civil servant, and following his defeat for that office continuing in his job as though nothing had happened. This is directly contrary to the whole concept of our civil service. It is contrary to the idea of the civil service being outside of politics, and being a body which serves the state rather than the political party which happens to be in power at any particular time. A few instances of this kind would soon destroy the morale of the civil service. The divorce of this body from politics would be at an end and, in effect, we would see the restoration of the old patronage system. The Minister of Agriculture is perhaps one of the few people in this country who would have a thing of this sort carried on, and then try 

to make out there was nothing out of the ordinary taking place; that he could not understand why people were raising the question.
The minister, having attempted to confuse this issue by interjecting irrelevant side issues, went on, and by the misuse of statistics tried to persuade the country that agriculture was in a very flourishing condition rather than in the somewhat depressed state the actual statistics reveal, and as I am sure the personal experience and knowledge of most members here would confirm. In regard to the reduction in farm income, which the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefen-baker) and others have brought to the attention of the government at this session, the minister said, and I quote from page 199 of Hansard for January 14, 1955:
What is the reduction in income in these three provinces-
Meaning the prairie provinces.
-because of wheat reduction in 1954 compared with the top year in that three-year period? . . . All told it is $440,900,000. That is the loss that has taken place in Saskatchewan, Alberta and Manitoba because of the fact that they had poor crops last year and low returns because of rust and low quality wheat.
I should like to emphasize that last phrase:
. . . because of the fact that they had poor crops last year and low returns because of rust and low quality wheat.
In other words, the minister was attempting to blame the weather for the reduction which took place in farm income in 1954. This is almost completely at variance with the facts. The reduction in farm income because of the poor crop of 1954 will show up chiefly in 1955. It did not show up last year to any extent. This is the year in which we are going to suffer from these poor crops last year.

He is trying to blame the weather for the butter situation, the cheese situation and so on. I shall have something to say about that later. The main point is that the deficiencies or defects shown in the government's agricultural policy have been largely to blame. The minister tries to find some other scapegoat, and apparently the weather is the one he can think of most readily.
As I have said, the real reason for the reduction in farm income in 1954 is our inability to sell a large proportion of the crop in 1953. Another reason was the lower price which was realized for the portion of the crop that was sold, plus higher storage
charges because the grain had to be kept in storage for a much longer period. Those are the two chief reasons for the lower farm income in 1954. The weather had very little to do with it.
Having quite incorrectly attempted to blame the weather for the reduced cash returns to the farmer, the minister then went on to say, and I quote again from page 199 of Hansard for January 14, 1955:
The total cash income in all the provinces of Canada in 1954 was $2,408 million and when you add to that the $444 million which the three wheat provinces lost last year because their crop was down and of a poor grade, you get a net return of $2,849 million. That is what the income would have been if they had had a good wheat delivery year and that is $23 million more than the farmers of this country ever had in any one year.
Before I go on to comment on that I must say that I do not know where the minister found this extra $4 million, because just a few sentences before he said it was $440 million and here he says it is $444 million. He suddenly found about $4 million more. Of course it is nothing for the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) to lose or find $4 million; he can lose or find hundreds of millions in his speeches depending on what he wants to say.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I did not use the figure $444 million, but it would be very easy for the typist to make that mistake.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
The minister should have
corrected it. I would be inclined to think that Hansard is correct because this is so typical of the sort of carelessness the minister exhibits so far as the use of figures is concerned.
This statement of the minister's which I have just read is a blatant attempt on his part to make this house and the country believe that the sales and prices of farm products are better than they ever were before. In other words, he is saying that the government has done its part and if only the weather had co-operated the farm population would never have been so well off. That is just another example of the well known "if" statement. In other words, if your aunt was not a woman she would be your uncle, and other statements along that line.
To put out nonsense of that kind, to say that if we had not had this crop failure, which I have demonstrated already had nothing to do with it, we would have had $440 million more of income and therefore the farmers would have been better off is doing no service to anyone and it certainly is doing no service to this house as it merely confuses the issue. I find it difficult to understand why the Minister of Agriculture persists in making statements of that nature.

The Address-Mr. Harkness
The reduction in farm income to which the minister devoted his attention was cash income, that is gross receipts. He did not touch on net income which is a much more important figure as far as the farmer is concerned. Just to take an example in another field. If you are running a store it is far better to have gross receipts of $100,000 and a profit of $10,000 than it is to have gross receipts or sales of $1,000,000 and a profit of only $5,000. It is exactly the same situation as far as the farmer is concerned.
It is not the gross receipts that he is primarily interested in. He is interested in them naturally, in the prices he gets and so forth, but the reason he is interested is that that is going to determine his net income to some extent. The thing he is really interested in, just the same as any other businessman, is his net income, the amount left over after all expenses, to be used to meet the needs of himself and his family for food, clothing and other necessities of life, to buy the luxuries which we all desire and to which it is considered we have some entitlement, to replace broken down or worn out farm machinery, to improve his farm and so on. The income he is interested in is his net income.
In dealing with this matter of farm income the minister said nothing about the farmers' net income. The reason he said nothing about it is that the figures are very grim indeed.

I gave the reason in my
speech why I did not use the net figures. You should read it.

That speech was just the same in that regard as most of the others: it was a sidestepping speech. As a matter of fact the minister did the same thing last year and the year before. He spoke of the cash income of the farmer but he carefully avoided going into the net income of the farmer.
I have the figures with reference to net income of our farmers. In 1951 it was $2,154,527,000; in 1952 it was $1,900,779,000, down $254 million. In 1953 it was $1,656564,000, down some $500 million from 1951. The figures are not out for this year but the general estimates of the farmers' net income that I have heard this year place it at no more than $1,400 million, and more likely it will be $1,200 million.
You can make a computation which will enable you to arrive at that pretty well from the figures of the past three years. Last year the difference between farm net income and cash income was $1,084,688,000. The spread has been getting worse every


year as the difference in 1951 was only $661,934,000. The spread this year is going to be more than $1,000 million, and most likely it will be about $1,200 million, leaving the farmer with a net income of about $1,200 million.
What that means is that the income which the farmer will have left over after expenses in 1954 will be just a little more than half of what he had for the same purposes in 1951. In other words his position is nearly 50 per cent worse in 1954 than it was in 1951.
However, the minister still tries to paint a rosy picture and he tells us that if it had not been for weather conditions our farmers would have had the biggest income this past year that they have ever had. With this situation confronting us it is no wonder that general business conditions last year were not as good as the year before. I would think that it is most doubtful that the rosy predictions of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) that things are going to be better than ever this year are likely to be realized with this very considerable reduction in farm net income with the consequent reduction in the amount of money which goes into the general stream of spending to provide employment and so forth.
After his speech in the house two weeks ago the minister went out west in the course of a few days, and demonstrated that he had by no means exhausted his ability to try to make black appear white, or at least a very pale grey. Even he admits that we have an oversupply of butter and cheese, but our surplus position was made worse by the importation of large quantities of New Zealand cheese. The only logical reason which might have been advanced for this importation was that it would help the forgotten man, the consumer, by giving him cheese at a lower price. However, the minister assured the dairy farmers that that would not happen. He said that the processing firm would be glad to make the dif-rence of five cents a pound between the price they would probably get that cheese at and the ordinary price at which cheese is selling. I can believe that the importing firm would be glad of that much extra profit.
But if this will be the result of this importation, what a ridiculous situation we have, Mr. Speaker. The price of butter is being supported by the taxpayers' money, and surpluses are being built up as a result of that to quite a large extent. Then this New Zealand cheese is imported to increase the surplus, because it can have no other effect

than to increase the surplus of dairy products in this country. The minister goes on to say that the importing firm will make an extra one-eighth to one-quarter million dollars, and that money is essentially to be paid by you and me, Mr. Speaker, and our fellow Canadians as taxpayers. The whole thing just does not make sense. If we are going to support the dairy industry by floor prices and sell the surplus, when we have a surplus as a result of that policy, at reduced prices to hospitals here, or to people in other countries, surely we should not let large amounts of dairy products from abroad come into the country at the same time. As a matter of fact, when we do that we in effect subsidize our competitors and the importing firm, so that we are taxing ourselves in order to subsidize our competitors in other countries and the importing firms which import these products.
As I say, the government just has no policy in regard to the dairy industry which makes sense. What it is doing is following the course of drift and bungle.

speechtext: Mostly bungle.

The farm income situation I have outlined is one of the main reasons for the large amount of unemployment we have had this winter. There are of course other reasons also. I am not one of those who make speeches, the purport of which is that the government can wave a magic wand and cure unemployment. I do not believe that the socialist wand would be effective in this regard, nor do I believe that the financial wand of the Social Crediters would be effective either. However, the government has done nothing in regard to the matter. They have just sat on their hands. Following the warning of last winter, which surely was stern enough as far as unemployment was concerned, the government has made no changes in its fiscal or financial policies which might have improved the unemployment picture, nor has it done any of the smaller specific things which might have helped, so far as I am aware.
As one small example of this failure, I was surprised to learn a short time ago that the government buys a considerable amount of its stationery requirements from the United States, all things which I believe are made in Canada, or if there are a few items which are not made in Canada they could certainly be purchased in Great Britain and thus help on the one hand to reduce our adverse balance of trade with the United States, and on the other hand to decrease Britain's adverse balance with us. I hold in my hand two forms used by the income tax
The Address-Mr. Harkness branch of the Department of National Revenue. They are complicated looking things. One of them is called an assessors' statistical report, and so forth, and the other has to do with instructions and the amount of adjustment. Hon. members can see that they are quite complicated looking forms, but they are a straight printing job; that is all they are. In each case, on the form in very small letters, so small that I can hardly read them, appears: "Printed in U.S.A." Why should the Department of National Revenue be making use of printed material of this sort which they import from the United States rather than having it printed in this country? As a matter of fact, that is not the end of this thing. In addition to these particular forms, I find that the government uses a large number of stationery items which are made in the United States. Some examples are staplers, staple pullers, Scripto pencil erasers, rubber finger pads, Scripto pencil leads, sensing leads, pencil sharpeners, and so on. As a matter of fact, if you go up to your office and look at your equipment which they supply us right in this building, if you look at the desk pen sets you will find stamped on the bottom-at least it is true of mine- "Made in U.S.A." The staplers are made in the U.S.A. too.
It seems to me this is something for which there is no excuse. It is carelessness on the part of the government. It is a lack of effort on their part to find small ways in which they can help to cure unemployment in this country. The total volume of Canadian employment which is lost this way must be quite large. This is only one small example of it. I know there must be a large number of items in which the same sort of thing is going on. If the government would devote some of its attention to plugging some of the small loopholes through which employment is lost in this country it might add up to quite considerable totals. Those are things which are entirely in their own hands.
To turn to another matter, I should like to reiterate the request made last year by the late Mr. Rodney Adamson that the committee on mines, forests and waters be given some work to do. This committee has been set up every year for a very long period, and within the memory of all hon. members here, with perhaps the exception of the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power), it has never done anything. It is just wasted motion setting up the committee and appointing members to it. It never meets in spite of the fact that the conservation and development of our natural resources are perhaps the most important things one can think of for the future of this country. I would suggest that this year the committee be given the

The Address-Mr. Campney task of investigating some important matter in the line of conservation or development. I would mention just two examples which they might investigate and report upon. One would be forest conservation and reforestation and the other would be the control and development of rivers.

Mr. Speaker, last fall I spent several weeks visiting our Canadian forces in Europe. I took occasion at that time to visit NATO headquarters in Paris as well as the supreme headquarters of allied powers in Europe or SHAPE as the military headquarters of NATO is commonly known. Again, in December last I attended the annual NATO council meeting in Paris. As a result of these experiences, which were in each case new experiences for me, I should like to give the house very briefly a few of my impressions of NATO and of Canada's relations to NATO.
I should think that NATO represents the greatest and most far-reaching attempt ever made in peacetime in the world to weld the military and economic forces of 14 sovereign nations into one cohesive, co-ordinated defence force for the defence of all. I think we may sometimes overlook the magnitude of the problems which NATO has undertaken. It is, from the very nature of the problem, a long-term project, and it is beset with very many difficulties: the language difficulty, for instance, the impact of national prejudice and misunderstanding, the differences in military outlook of the component nations, the variability of the strategical and tactical conception of the military forces and the lack of standardization of military equipment.
These are only a few of the practical factors which combine to slow up and to complicate the achievement of NATO's goal. And yet I believe that great results in fact have already been attained by NATO. Slowly but steadily we are evolving a strong, united and well integrated defence force in Europe.
I was tremendously impressed with the manoeuvre "Battle Royal" which I attended last fall in north Germany. There were 140,000 troops, British and Dutch, on the one side, and French, Belgian and Canadian on the other side, each side working together as a team and doing so very smoothly and successfully. It constituted, to me at least, a very vivid commentary on the progress being made in the welding together of NATO forces.
On the planning and organizational side, too, steady progress is in fact being made. Greater mutual understanding is being engendered and formidable obstacles, one after the other, are being steadily overcome.

I believe it is very fortunate for us all that NATO had a few years in which to set and become seasoned before we were faced by the full impact of the power of atomic and thermonuclear weapons. If this' had not been so the organization would hardly have been complete enough to make it possible for the supreme allied commander to make the very careful and far-reaching analysis of the thermonuclear threat which, through the military committee, he gave to the NATO council last December when it met in Paris, together with the outline of necessary plans to enable the NATO military forces to meet that threat.
These plans, of course, do not derogate in any way from the responsibilities of the governments of the countries comprising NATO in regard to the decision which is theirs alone as to how and when military action is to be authorized. This forward-looking report was only the first of such reports to be made in sequence as the mihtary studies continue.
My general impression of the defence side of the NATO council meeting was that of steady progress in all fields of military endeavour. There is, of course, much to be accomplished. There are many unsolved problems still remaining, but the fact that these difficult and intricate defence questions are being tackled and solved in a clear, vigorous and orderly fashion is to me very encouraging indeed.
The analysis of the planning which went to make up the report to which I have referred is, of course, secret, and therefore its contents cannot be disclosed. However, as there has been considerable speculation in the press about the matter I would like to assure the house that we do not contemplate any immediate drastic reorganization of our Canadian forces as a result of these studies. Nor do we contemplate any increase in our commitment to NATO forces.
There is no doubt that there will be certain shifts of emphasis and some new developments, but nothing of a revolutionary character. Obviously, the introduction of new weapons and new techniques has greatly increased the pace and the destructive power of future warfare, and priority, therefore, is being given to the raising, training, and equipment of forces described as "forces in being," that is, forces which must be immediately ready to take their place in the battle line.
Increased emphasis, too, is being placed on the air arm, but as hon. members are well aware this increased emphasis on air power is and has been for some years past a feature of our own Canadian defence program.
In this regard the military committee of NATO has been continually stressing for some time past the need for increased air defence

in Europe, particularly in the field of allweather fighters. We have been pressed for some time past to assist in this regard by reason of the fact that we in Canada are producing, in the CF-100, what is generally regarded as one of the very best all-weather fighters in NATO.
The government, after careful consideration, has decided that as soon as our regular air defence squadrons in Canada are completely equipped with CF-lOO's, which will be during the present year, we will be able- that is next year-to take steps toward meeting the pressing need of NATO for allweather fighters.
We do not propose to provide any over-all increase in the number of squadrons in our air force in Europe, which will remain at 12 squadrons as at present, but we are prepared to replace the aircraft in four of our day fighter squadrons in the air division in Europe with CF-100 all-weather fighters. This step will very materially strengthen the allweather defence capabilities of the NATO forces and thus help to meet one of NATO's most urgent needs.
It will also, by having the same types of aircraft in operational squadrons at home and abroad, make for maximum efficiency and economy, and will enable the R.C.A.F. to gain the broadest possible experience in allweather operations.
As a component nation of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization Canada has carried out her commitments in detail and on time. That should be a source of justifiable pride to all of us.
I cannot refrain from a brief word of comment on the quality of the forces we have supplied to NATO. Last fall, as I said, I spent three weeks in Europe, during which time I visited every unit of our first infantry brigade and each of the 12 squadrons which make up our air division. They are both a credit to Canada.
There is, I feel sure, no finer, more modernly equipped, better trained fighting air force in Europe today than the Canadian air division, equipped with Canadian-built Sabre jet planes powered by Canadian-built Orenda engines. When the squadrons have all been equipped with Sabre mark VI, they will be still more effective.
The men of the first infantry brigade are well trained, healthy, and of high morale. Their relationship with the German civilian population is exemplary. They won high praise from the umpires of "Battle Royal" for their initiative, for effectiveness and for endurance.
The Address-Mr. Campney
Notwithstanding the increased emphasis being placed on air development, there is, I believe, no question but that the army will continue to play an important part in our defence picture.
The emphasis may have changed, but the importance of the army's function remains. Changes in organization and tactical disposition may well become necessary. Devastating thermonuclear weapons may lead to a greater dispersal of manpower, smaller units, different types of weapons, and streamlined lines of communication. But an effective defensive barrier on the ground will always be needed where there is a threat of ground attack.
The advent of mass destruction weapons does not eliminate the need for conventional forces in all forms of warfare, great and small, and the army will continue to be required to play its historic and important role in any war of the future.
The same reasoning will, I believe, continue to apply to our naval forces. The supply line between North America and Europe must be kept open. That is of vital importance to all of us. The submarine menace which has so often nearly defeated us must in any future war be mastered and kept in check. The days of the battleship may be numbered, but the comparatively small very fast submarine killer will be more necessary than ever.
We in Canada are therefore, in keeping with our undertaking to NATO, building the most modern destroyer escorts we can devise, and we are modernizing our frigates, minesweepers, and other small craft to provide a fast powerful fleet for convoy duty and to meet the new Snorkel submarines being built in such great numbers by our only prospective enemy.
Thus we must maintain and keep modern and effective our conventional forces on both land and sea. The necessity of strong conventional NATO forces is fully exemplified by the importance we all attach to the 12 divisions we expect West Germany to provide for NATO when the protocol which was approved by the house a few days ago has been fully ratified and becomes effective.
The defence of Canada-indeed of North America-has suddenly become almost as important to the other NATO nations as it has always been to ourselves. This fact arises, of course, from the emergence of an improved Russian nuclear weapon delivery capability against North America. Under such circumstances it becomes essential that greater efforts be put forth immediately to strengthen the defences of this continent because North America is the only great base

The Address-Mr. Campney from which operations for the defence of Europe can be supported, and also because of the necessity of protecting the thermonuclear retaliatory capacity of the United States, something which provides at the present time probably the greatest single deterrent to war.
And so what we have come to term "continental defence", that great joint effort of Canada and the United States to protect and to defend both countries against aggressive attack, is at the same time a very real and vital contribution to NATO's effort as well. Thus every dollar we spend on "continental defence" has a double value. It has value first and primarily, of course, for our own defence and, second, for the preservation of the defence capacity of NATO as a whole.
"Continental defence" is an expensive business. The so-called "Pinetree" radar chain now in operation, supported by the fighter squadrons of air defence command, along with the mid-Canada line which Canada is proceeding to construct and the distant warning line to be constructed in the far north, together form a comprehensive air defence system and will cost many hundreds of millions of dollars. A large portion of the cost of this system is still to be paid. This cost will entail a very considerable drain on Canada's resources during the next few years.
In passing I should like to express to our friends to the south our appreciation of the very fine spirit of co-operation and understanding shown in the development of this great defensive system, on the construction of which we are jointly engaged.

As far as my department is concerned, the decision is that the value that would be obtained defence-wise would not justify the cost of the project as compared with other defence projects. We have turned this suggestion down, as far as defence is concerned, on several occasions.
Our relations with our neighbour demonstrate how easy it is for peoples with like ideals and with common incentives to work 
closely and effectively together in peace and harmony to their mutual benefit. I was deeply appreciative of defence secretary Wilson's statement yesterday in Washington which I think bears out what I have just said.
In concluding these few brief remarks I should like to emphasize the fact that Canada's military effort is motivated solely by considerations of self-protection. We have no aggressive designs against any other nation. We covet no nation's territory. We have never initiated a war against anyone. We are, in fact, not a warlike people, though we can fight if we have to. Our present effort is a defence effort only. It is an effort which we are making in the hope that it will contribute to the joint strength of the NATO nations whose only aim is peace.
I have mentioned how much I was impressed when I was in Germany last fall with the close and friendly relations which existed between our troops and their families and the German people of the area in which they are stationed. I might give one small incident to illustrate what I mean. Pending the completion of our married quarters in Westphalia, many of our soldiers' families lived with Germans in German homes. As an example of the co-operation which existed, I might mention that while I was there I met the burgomaster of Soest and his school officials at a German school in which they had crowded together the German children, voluntarily, so as to empty several rooms for the children of soldiers while our schools were being completed. I visited the children in those schoolrooms and saw them being taught by our Canadian teachers operating in the German schools. This is merely an example or an indication of the friendly and co-operative feeling which was generally evident. Yet less than 10 years ago these people were our bitter enemies, and we were their bitter enemies.
It seems to me that all of us might derive a lesson from that example. If we could only establish with the Russian people as individuals such personal contact and understanding as our soldiers and their families in Germany have established with the German people, perhaps the prospect of war might rapidly fade. Probably history will record as the greatest of all the crifnes which the Russian dictatorship has perpetrated against humanity the forced isolation of its people from contact with the rest of the world. Perhaps one day this monstrous imprisonment of a whole people can be overcome. If it is ever possible to overcome that imprisonment, I believe that the fear of war might rapidly abate.
In the meantime, the maintenance of peace is dependent on the continuing build-up of

effective military strength of the free nations. We must become so strong collectively that no one will attack us. That is the goal of NATO. What the 14 nations which comprise NATO-and we hope the admission of Western Germany will soon make it 15-could not hope to do individually, we can, I believe, accomplish by determined collective effort.
It is the function of NATO leaders to develop and fully to integrate that effort so that it may attain the highest possible degree of effectiveness alike in immediate availability of defence and in retaliatory capacity. From my own observation I believe that those directing NATO will measure up to the requirements of that most important task.

Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to ask the minister a question although I realize there are many questions in which we are all interested and we could probably keep him answering them all afternoon. I do wish to congratulate him on having been appointed head of the department and to wish him every success. May I say that I agree entirely with what he has said with reference to NATO because I am sure our hopes and the hopes for peace in this world are bound up to a very great extent with the success of NATO.
Many members have already spoken in the debate on the speech from the throne. Many subjects have been discussed and perhaps there are few left, but it does not seem to be out of the way to repeat things in this debate. While many subjects have been discussed, we still have the problems with us and I am sure we all realize that speaking on these questions does not in any way solve our problems. As usual the throne speech this year mentions many of our problems, both world-wide and national. Unfortunately, we do not find in it very many solutions for the problems we have.
One of the first matters dealt with in the house was the ratification of the Paris agreements. This was mentioned in the throne speech. While I did not speak on the ratification of these agreements, may I say now that I am in entire accord with the solution contained in them that was approved by the house. We also discussed the serious unemployment situation in Canada, and while no solution was put forward during that debate the problem was nevertheless very thoroughly discussed.
We have, as usual, more than our share of unemployment in the maritime provinces. I am not going to discuss that now except to mention and pay tribute to the efforts made by two towns in the province of New Brunswick which were faced over a year ago with very serious unemployment. I refer first to the town of Marysville in the province of New Brunswick where Canadian Cottons closed their cotton mill over a year ago. The people of the town derived almost 100 per cent of their employment from the cotton

The Address-Mr. Brooks factory. After the factory was closed these people did not move away to other parts of Canada or other parts of our own province. They undertook to try to solve their own problems. They were faced with heavy taxes. Marysville has splendid schools, and anyone who has been there knows that it is a splendid up-to-date town.
The people sought employment wherever they could find it, and I might tell the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Campney) that many of the men found employment at the Gagetown camp. However, they have to travel 25 to 30 miles morning and night in order to work at the camp, and they deserve great credit for doing so.
The other day an hon. member said that it was up to the people of the maritimes to try to solve their own problems. The town of Milltown is an instance of where that has been done. When the factory there was closed hundreds of men were thrown out of employment. They decided that they would solve their own problem. Instead of going to other parts of Canada they decided to try to open the factory and run it on a co-operative basis, which they were successful in doing. I am proud to say that as the result of this co-operative effort the workers of Milltown have employment today.
Much has been said in the debate about our loss of markets. This of course is one of the great problems of Canada. Loss of markets means loss of employment. Comment has been made here on the fact that after the war Canada and the United States had practically a clear field so far as the markets of the world were concerned. It was no effort for Canadian manufacturers or producers to sell their products in the markets of the world. It was no effort for the people of the United States to do so. The factories of Germany were destroyed and she had to go about securing new machines. The same was true to a lesser extent in Great Britain and was also true in France, Italy and Japan.
But today we have to face competition from all these countries and there is a grave fear in Canada that we are not facing up to the competition. I am reminded of a story I heard the other day of a South American country that was seeking certain heavy machinery to instal in a plant in that country. The owner of the factory wrote to Great Britain, France, the United States, Canada and Germany. The story is that from Great Britain there came a letter saying that they had the best and finest machinery in the world. France did not make any reply. The United States and Canada sent catalogues. However, in a short time two engineers from Germany arrived with the machinery and


asked where they might instal it. That story may or may not be true, but we do know that today the German people are taking over the South American market to a great extent. We also know that what is true of South America is true of many other parts of the world. Canada and the United States are losing markets which they so easily held during the post-war years.
If I may say so, it does seem to me that the time has arrived for Canadian manufacturers, producers, labour leaders and government officials to get together, because unless they do so I am satisfied that many of the markets which we have had will be lost to us for one reason or another.
The speech from the throne also gave a detailed statement of many undertakings. There was mention of the St. Lawrence seaway and hydro development. So far as I can see, this will be of no great benefit to us in the maritime provinces. As I said last year, and as I repeat now, the maritime provinces have no objection to the development of the St. Lawrence seaway. They have no objection to the great benefits which will be derived by the people of Ontario and Quebec as a result of the development of hydro power in the international waters.
The speech from the throne mentioned the Canso causeway. This is a good thing for Nova Scotia. They have waited for it for many years, and no one is more pleased than the people of New Brunswick that it is now an accomplished fact. It will be of very little benefit to the people of New Brunswick. We have heard of the Bar Harbor ferry and that also will be of benefit to Nova Scotia. We rejoice that Nova Scotia has received this recognition which will result in a great increase in the tourist trade of that province. As one of the Nova Scotia members said the other day, it will unquestionably mean more trade between Nova Scotia and the New England states. No benefit will be derived by New Brunswick; as a matter of fact I believe it will take away much of the tourist trade we now enjoy, coming in through St. Stephen and going through to Saint John and the various parts of New Brunswick.
Again the speech from the throne mentions the Sydney-Port aux Basques ferry. This also is a good thing. I could go on through the long catalogue of these many things. Mention was made of Ripple Rock in British Columbia, about which I have heard ad nauseam, I might say, from the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green). I congratulate him and the other members from that province on the fact this rock will be removed.

All these undertakings, Mr. Speaker, will not relieve the unemployment situation in this country, nor are they going to provide markets for our people. A short time ago I was interested in reading in the Labour Research a long account of the economic trends in the Atlantic provinces. The author posed many questions and supplied many answers. The first question which he asked was, what has been happening to the three old maritime provinces since the end of the war, or the four Atlantic provinces since Newfoundland became a member in 1949? He answers the question by saying that everyone knows they are less prosperous than the rest of the country. He then asks, are they catching up or falling farther behind or just holding their place in the race?
The dominion bureau of statistics gives the answer for the three maritime provinces. In 1946, personal income per head was $177 or 22 [DOT] 3 per cent below the national average. By 1949 it was $287 or 30-2 per cent below the national average; 1953, $406 or 32-3 per cent below the national average. At the end of the war, the gap was already considerable. Last year, it was about 50 per cent worse.
Another question was, are they getting a larger or smaller share of the national income? This question is easily answered. According to the bureau of statistics we are about 27 per cent lower than the Canadian average. Is employment keeping pace with the national indices, or better or worse? Nova Scotia with 45 per cent of the employment in the maritime provinces has never kept pace with the national index since 1946. New Brunswick, with 30 per cent, has lagged behind the national figure every year. Taking the three maritime provinces together, there can be no question that the increase in employment since the end of the war has been very small, far smaller than the country as a whole. Wages have fallen below the national average.
As I said a few minutes ago, when there is unemployment in Canada unfortunately the percentage of unemployment is always greater for the four Atlantic provinces than any other section of the country. According to the dominion bureau of statistics the figures for 37 dates, from October 1949 to November 1954, show that on every date the percentage of unplaced applicants was above the national percentage, usually considerably above. For 1950, it averaged over 60 per cent higher; for 1951, almost 36 per cent; for 1952, almost 31 per cent; for 1953, almost 47 per cent; and for the first 11 months of 1954, almost 28 per cent.
The Address-Mr. Brooks
The article also takes up the question of farming, fishing, mining, etc. I shall not take the time of the house to discuss those industries this afternoon, except to say that in only one instance, that is fisheries, had the maritime provinces more than held their own during the past few years.
Now, I come to one of the recommendations in the amendment offered by our acting leader (Mr. Rowe). It reads as follows:
(e) To facilitate and encourage the processing of our natural resources in Canada, and thereby increase opportunities and employment for Canadians;
I am 100 per cent behind that recommendation, Mr. Speaker. I have been advocating that for a good many years in this house. We in the province of New Brunswick believe implicitly in it. We believe that there are great potentialities, great opportunities in our province today. I do not wish to weary the house by repeating what has been said by members from New Brunswick during the last two years about the great natural resources, the great mineral deposits which have been found in the Bathurst area of New Brunswick. Last year in the Little River area north of the town of Newcastle they discovered even greater mineral deposits, including over three million tons of base metals, rich in copper, zinc and lead, etc.
Recently there has been a find near Woodstock which is reported to contain 150 million tons of manganese. I know, as other members know, that manganese is a very important mineral so far as the steel industry is concerned. I can recall during the first war, when we received most of our manganese from across the water, every effort was made to find manganese in this country. Little pockets here and there were dug and used. In the second great war efforts were made to find more of this mineral. Today, in the province of New Brunswick, we have 150 million tons of manganese which will be of great importance to a country so interested in the development of steel. I believe all hon. members will agree that minerals in the ground are of no value; they have to be mined. There have been millions and millions of tons of iron ore in Labrador for millions of years. A railroad has been extended into that area and those millions of tons of ore will be brought out and smelted. This means riches, not only for that part of the country but for the world in general.
There is not much benefit to any province or any locality if minerals are simply dug out of the ground and moved to some other place to be smelted. When that is done you are simply being hewers of wood and drawers of water. What we would like to have and

The Address-Mr. Brooks what we should have in New Brunswick are smelters which will process these great rich finds of minerals which we have.
When I asked the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) why it was that we did not have decentralization of industry or more industry in our province he has told me on more than one occasion that the one essential was cheap electric power. We have suffered in New Brunswick in the past because we did not have cheap electric power in order to develop our resources or to manufacture in competition with other parts of Canada.
Now that these great mineral deposits have been found, our province will suffer even more unless cheap electric power is developed in New Brunswick. It will be noted from what I have said that New Brunswick is facing both an opportunity and a dilemma. Until cheap electric power is developed the maritime provinces, and New Brunswick in particular, will lag behind the rest of Canada. We have had neither the power nor the resources to do otherwise.
We know that there is enough undeveloped power in our province to make it potentially and economically sound and prosperous to exploit fully these newly found resources of mineral wealth as well as to develop the future manufacture of our raw materials. But we must have cheap power in relative plenty. This is now known to be available in the Saint John river and possibly on the Passa-maquoddy.
I refer to the Passamaquoddy because the state of Maine wishes to have an investigation made of the possibility of using the tides for power development. I hope that it will be found practical. I hope that the Dominion of Canada will join with the United States in endeavouring to find out whether the development of the Passamaquoddy is a practical proposition. If power were to be developed there it would assist not only New Brunswick but all of the maritime provinces.
There is a great opportunity to start an industrial revolution in our maritimes economy. There is the usual problem, particularly for a small and poorer province like New Brunswick, which is ill equipped to finance the development of cheap power which is necessary for this other development. Our public debt has reached proportions where it absorbs nearly one-quarter of the provincial government expenditures just for service charges. Our population is small, it being hardly half that of the city of Toronto, but it is bearing this burden with a per capita income which is less than 60 per cent of that of Ontario.
Because we have not cheap power, industry has ignored our province for a great many years. As I said a moment ago, we have been asking continually for the decentralization of industry. We have been told repeatedly that there cannot be decentralization of industry until cheap power is available because industry will not go where there is no cheap power.
As I stated in the house at the last session, I believe that the immediate answer to our power problem is the development of power sites on the Saint John river, particularly at Beechwood. If there was a proper financing of the development at Beechwood it would start a downward trend in power costs and would affect the whole provincial industrial picture.
The provincial government has undertaken the development of Beechwood but it will cost $45 million or more. To go to the money market to finance this project would mean almost prohibitive power costs. It would not then be possible to attract the industrial development we desire in the province. I understand that the provincial government has come to Ottawa and said in effect, "Will the nation as a whole help us with this difficult problem? Once we have taken this big step we feel we will be able to go on by ourselves."
I understand that the provincial government is seeking a loan from the federal government for a period of years at a small interest rate. It is not seeking a handout, it is seeking a loan that would be repaid and which would be used for something that would be of great benefit to us. I have not seen any of the correspondence between the federal government and the provincial government but my understanding is that Ottawa feels it is not right or proper to give help along these lines for the development of provincial resources.
No doubt that is technically right, but on examining many of the activities of the federal government over the past year in different parts of Canada I find that assistance has been given to certain projects in areas which had no better claim than this, and, I feel, not as good.
As I said a few moments ago, we are assisting in the development of the St. Lawrence seaway which will not be of any direct benefit to the maritime provinces. We have paid out millions of dollars under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) may reply that we have had assistance in connection with our marshlands, but for every dollar we have

received for the repair of our dikes I venture to say that $100 has gone to the western provinces.
I spoke about the Canso causeway a few moments ago and how pleased I was that Nova Scotia had received this great benefit. That is another proposition which is more or less akin to this assistance in the development of hydro power in New Brunswick.
A few years ago when the situation was so serious in Great Britain, they had what were known as depressed areas. I was pleased to read reports indicating that the government of that day decided to help these sections in Wales and Durham and other parts of England by bringing in industry, thereby attempting to bring those areas up to a level of prosperity with the rest of the country.
I think something of that kind should be done in Canada. The Minister of Agriculture mentioned the South Saskatchewan dam the other day. I understood him to say that perhaps it would go through some day. Power development is needed more by the maritime provinces than is the South Saskatchewan dam, in the west, but we in New Brunswick and the maritime provinces will raise no objections if he desires to go ahead with that proposition.
I do not think it is necessary, but the house may be interested in a few newspaper articles I have here dealing with what I have been saying. In the Maritime Merchant of January of this year there is an editorial headed "Power is the Key to Industrial Expansion", which reads:
The paper mill of the New Brunswick International Paper Company at Dalhousie, New Brunswick, is said to use five times more power than the city of Saint John.
The problem facing the Hearst newspaper organization in considering establishment of a $10,000,000 mill on Nova Scotia's eastern shore is said to be largely one of power supply.
Think of what that would mean to Nova Scotia. Mr. L. R. Riggs, the manager of the Brunswick Mining and Smelting Corporation Limited, when speaking before the Gloucester county council at Bathurst the other day, had this to say:
The problem of whether or not there is to be a refinery in New Brunswick depends largely on the availability of cheap power in large quantities. Mr. Riggs gave as an example that their zinc smelter owned and operated by St. Joseph's Lead in Josephtown, Pa., used more electrical power in 1954 than was developed by the New Brunswick hydro commission in the same year.
He stated that he was informed that Beechwood and the entire Saint John river proposed development would not have sufficient firm power to operate a similar type smelter in addition to the normal growth of the power demands for the province.
Professor William Y. Smith, head of the department of economics at the University of
The Address-Mr. Brooks New Brunswick, when speaking to the council of the Saint John board of trade a short time ago said:
From being one of the depressed or "have-not" provinces New Brunswick can expand and take its proper place as one of the provinces with a high and rising standard of living.
He mentioned the great mineral deposits and discoveries in the province and went on to say:
The development of these mineral deposits can work a revolution in the provincial economy provided that they are developed in such a way as to be of maximum benefit to the province. The more refining and smelting of the ore which can be done within the province the greater will be the increase in incomes which will accrue to the people of New Brunswick.
This is the important part:
To take advantage of our opportunity we need but one thing-large quantities of relatively cheap power. Almost one-quarter of all electricity consumed in Canada is used by mining, smelting and refining industries. New Brunswick must have more power; cheap power, together with proper use of our known resources, is the key to our future. By 1957 estimated normal demand for power will exceed the installed capacity of the New Brunswick Electric Power Commission.
I am not going to labour that point any further, Mr. Speaker. I should now like to say a few words about the army camp in New Brunswick.
The Minister	of	Labour spoke	to	the
Fredericton retail merchants association a while ago and is reported in the press as follows:
Mr. Gregg said	the	business section	and	thewhole camp area	was	to become not	only	an
integral part of the life of this immediate community but of New Brunswick as a whole.
Perhaps he had been receiving pressure from the city of Fredericton and other areas for special consideration. Gagetown camp is mostly in my constituency. Of the 1,100 people who were displaced and scattered over all parts of New Brunswick and Canada, over three-quarters of them came from the county of Queens, which is part of the constituency of Royal. These people are very well settled at the present time. I have discussed the matter before, but what I wish to impress upon the government, and especially upon the Minister of Defence Production (Mr. Howe), is that while we in New Brunswick cannot supply the millions of dollars' worth of clothing, boots and shoes, vehicles, guns and all that sort of thing that will come from Ontario and Quebec and from other parts of Canada, we can supply most of the food that is needed in this camp. For instance, there is no need to go to other parts of Canada than the maritime provinces to get the fish that is required for the troops who will be stationed there. My constituency is a great

The Address-Mr. Brooks dairy constituency and all the milk and butter required for Camp Gagetown can and should be obtained from the surrounding area.
I am pleased indeed to know that the heating apparatus for the different housing units is of such a nature that it will use New Brunswick coal. I suggested that in this house on several occasions and the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) nods his head in affirmation of the fact that we are to use Minto coal. I congratulate the Department of National Defence on this. It will be a great boon to the coal-producing area of New Brunswick, which is partly in my constituency and partly in the constituency of the Minister of Labour.
Take fruits. You never hear very much about New Brunswick apples in this house, but I am sure the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), if he has eaten New Brunswick McIntosh Reds-and if he has not he has missed a lot-will say that in the Saint John river valley we grow the finest apples that are grown anywhere in this Dominion of Canada. There is no reason why the fruit that is necessary for Camp Gagetown should not all be purchased in the surrounding area. The same thing applies to small fruits, berries. Large quantities of strawberries and other berries are grown in and around the camp area.
Instead of being pessimistic in my speech I like to be optimistic. I was pleased to see a report a few days ago that the coal industry in New Brunswick had been prosperous last year. The answer is in the fact that the New Brunswick government is using as much provincial coal as possible. I commend them for it; I commend the federal government for its intention to use New Brunswick coal in the army camp. The pulp mills in New Brunswick have become extensive users of coal, and they have also purchased equipment so they can use our own New Brunswick coal. For this I commend them. The result is that that industry is on its own feet and is in a prosperous condition in New Brunswick.
I have some other notes but I see that my time is nearly up. The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Regier) was down to our province last summer, and we are very glad to have members from other parts of Canada visit us. We have had a great many of them, and I am sure they are always welcome. Some praise us but most tell us how we should run our province. I should like to say this. We do not tell the other provinces how to run their business; what we do is send our people there who run it for them.
As an instance, the premier of British Columbia-this may not be popular-was a pupil of mine when I taught school in New Brunswick. At least three other premiers of the province of British Columbia came from the province of New Brunswick. The chief justice of British Columbia, the province from which this gentleman came and told us how to run our province, came from my constituency. The chief forester-and these are only a few that I can think of at the present time-came from the province of New Brunswick. The head of the Roman Catholic church in British Columbia, Archbishop Duke, is a New Brunswicker. Three of the six senators came from the province of New Brunswick, and two of them from my own constituency, I could go on, Mr. Speaker, and name many more notables who have come from our province and helped look after the government not only in British Columbia but in other provinces in this dominion. We also sent a prime minister to Great Britain, the only one, I believe, to come from any other part of the commonwealth. He came from New Brunswick.

I have now completed my remarks, Mr. Speaker, and I wish to thank hon. members for their very kind attention. I hope the government will take under serious consideration some method by which they can help us to help ourselves without costing the taxpayers of this country any considerable amount of money.
Mr. F. G. Robertson (Northumberland, Oni.k
Mr. Speaker, I would like to join with other hon. members in extending my congratulations to the mover (Mr. Leduc) and seconder (Mr. Carrick) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I also wish to congratulate the government for foreshadowing legislation having to do with increases in the war veterans allowance and the income ceiling, as well as the liberalization of the Blind Persons Act. Both these measures will be much appreciated by the vast majority of Canadians, and I know the veterans themselves will indeed be thankful to the government for this action. As one member who has felt that this action should be taken as soon as economic conditions would permit, I am happy to see that this has now been done.
As the parliamentary representative for the county of Northumberland, wherein one-half of the people derive their income from agriculture, I naturally have great concern for the welfare of our farmers. It is a matter of note that the income of farmers during

the past ten years has been the highest on record. While we regret that there has been some falling off in income during the last two or three years, we believe this is not nearly as serious as some opposition members would have us believe. In fact, farm leaders themselves would be quite satisfied, in most cases, if present conditions could continue. I realize that the income of Canadian farmers as a whole is down, but I am happy to point out that, upon checking the income of Ontario farmers, I have found there was an increase of $49,233,000 in their income for 1954 over their income for 1953. This was largely brought about by increased prices for hogs, cattle, tobacco and similar products.
One branch of agriculture which has some reason for concern at the present time is the dairy industry, and I am happy to note that the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) a few days ago brought to the attention of this house the importance of the dairy industry to agriculture as a whole in Canada.
I am pleased to note that the government has continued its support program, because this has been most helpful not only to the Canadian farmer but in bolstering economic stability throughout the country. At the present time we have a support price program for eggs, butter, and hogs, and that program has played an important part in stabilizing our economy. I would point out that the cost of this program has been relatively low. On the support of farm products we have spent $80,163,658.71, of which some $69 million was spent because of foot-and-mouth disease in Canada. If we subtract the latter amount it will be seen that by the expenditure of some $11 million we have done much to stabilize agriculture in this country.
No part of our Canadian economy is more dependent upon international trade than is agriculture. The government is continually doing all it can to stimulate international trade and I would commend the government for its efforts in this regard.
