The hon. member is not quite so well informed on agriculture as he may be on labour matters, and even there I question whether he is very much of an authority.
International trade, however, is not a oneway street. We cannot expect to export unless we import, and I think the government realizes this fact and that is the reason for the action they have taken.
I would ask the government to continue their assistance to the dairy industry, and I would also urge them to continue the support price for butter. I was very pleased indeed to learn today that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) has recommended to the government that some of the surplus butter be taken off the open market, and that action will be taken in this regard. I think this will do much to stabilize the dairy industry in Canada. I would also ask the government to continue the support price of 58 cents per pound for butter after the termination of the present plan. I know it is not necessary to ask them to continue their efforts in promoting world trade whenever possible.
I should like now to say a few words regarding civil defence in Canada in the light of the knowledge which has recently become available, particularly with regard to the development of the hydrogen bomb. Let me say at the outset, Mr. Speaker, that I do not envy the task of those who are burdened with the responsibility for the development of a civil defence organization, whether it be on a federal, provincial, or municipal level. Those who are working in this field face extraordinary problems at all levels, and they must, I am sure, suffer extreme frustration.
I suggest though, Mr. Speaker, that Canada has made good progress in developing a civil defence organization. We have a well organized civil defence system on the federal and provincial levels, and in many of our larger cities and even some of the smaller communities. I think we can say it is comparable with the best of any other nation, though I do not argue for one moment that there is not yet much to be done. It is interesting to point out that the' federal budget for civil defence has grown from $872,000 in the year 1951-52 to over $7 million during the present year.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) has enunciated two basic principles having to do with civil defence in Canada. The first is that civil defence is essentially a civilian activity, quite separate and distinct from the national preparations which are necessary to defend this country by
638	HOUSE OF COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Robertson
military action in the event of war. The second is that civil defence is the general concern of all levels of government. There is an important role for every level of government in developing measures for the protection of their civilian populations, measures which must draw on the federal, provincial and local facilities and services. I should like to quote President Eisenhower's inaugural state of the nation address in 1953, when he discussed the last mentioned question:
Civil defence responsibilities primarily belong to the state and local governments-recruiting, training and organizing volunteers to meet any emergency. The immediate job of the federal government is to provide leadership, to supply technical guidance and to continue to strengthen its civil defence stockpile of medical, engineering and related supplies and equipment.
Our federal government takes the same view, and in my opinion this is the only course possible. The federal government is acting as the planning, the guiding and the co-ordinating agency, but I think everyone agrees that the operational responsibility rests with the local authorities. Any other approach to this matter would be inconsistent with our conception of jurisdictional rights in Canada. It would represent an unwarranted intrusion upon provincial and local rights and would make for inefficiency if the federal government, for instance, should try to take charge of a community's fire, police and health services.
The financial arrangements have been changed within the last year. Under the new regulations federal aid can be given to municipalities undertaking civil defence projects regardless of whether provincial assistance is available, and it can be increased to double the basic amount for any project for which provincial assistance is available.
I should now like to give you some of the highlights of the federal program, which I feel is full of worth-while accomplishments. More than $2 million worth of civil defence training supplies and equipment have been provided to provincial and local organizations. This includes 15 fully-equipped rescue vehicles, 50 fully-equipped mobile fire pumpers, and 100,000 service type respirators. An extensive series of training manuals, films, exhibits and other educational material has been produced and made available without charge to provincial and local civil defence organizations.
A number of operational exercises have been carried out, of which the most far-reaching, "Operation Alert", was undertaken in co-operation with the civil defence authorities in the United States, to test the effectiveness of civil defence organizations in some 50 cities in our two countries.

A permanent civil defence college capable of training 2,000 instructors and key workers each year has been established at Arnprior. Special committees are engaged in working out detailed plans for the most effective use of transportation facilities, communications, health services, welfare services and so on.
To ensure co-operation with other friendly nations, Canada has become a member of the NATO civil defence co-ordinating committee, and federal civil defence officials meet regularly with their United States counterparts on the joint United States-Canada civil defence committee.
Agreements to share in providing compensation for injury to civil defence workers have been entered into with three provinces and the offer of federal assistance is still open to all the other provinces. Over 400 air raid sirens have been supplied to target areas exclusively at federal expense, and most of these have been installed with the federal authority sharing in the cost of installation under certain conditions.
The defence research board and other federal agencies are actively engaged on a number of research projects related to A B C defence, including the use of blood substitutes, shock therapy, weapons' effects and radiation detection.
The federal government has spent in the neighbourhood of $400,000 as a contribution of one-third of the cost of standardizing hose couplings in British Columbia, Alberta and Ontario. Every encouragement is offered to the other provinces to take advantage of this standing offer of federal assistance.
We live today in a hydrogen bomb age and there can be no doubt that if atomic science can be used for the betterment of mankind, we face a period of great happiness. If, however, it is used for war, then we face a period of unknown tragedy. I should like to quote to you what Senator Brien McMahon had to say with regard to this problem. He said in part as follows:
It is our solemn obligation, I think, to lift our eyes above the lesser problems that seem to monopolize our time and to discuss and act upon what, by any standard, is the supreme problem before our country and the world.
It has been suggested by some people in this and other countries that the hydrogen bomb has made civil defence obsolete. Nothing could be further from the truth. I should like to bring to your attention the opinions of such men as Sir Winston Churchill, who said the hydrogen bomb made the need for civil defence even greater than ever; Sir John Hodsoll, who is director of the NATO civil defence committee; Sir Sidney Kirkman, who is director general of civil

defence in the United Kingdom; and General Gruenther, commander in chief of the NATO forces. All these distinguished and able men say that the need for civil defence is as great as or greater than ever. I should like to quote part of what the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. St. Laurent) had to say, writing in the special supplement of the civil defence bulletin in January, 1955:
We have all heard people say that because of the hydrogen bomb civil defence is obsolete. This to me seems like a hopeless and thoughtless attitude that can only mean greater destruction and loss of life if war should come. True, the hydrogen bomb is a terrible weapon. True, its use would mean many casualties and great suffering but it seems to me that this vastly greater destructive power calls for vastly greater effort, not for a hopeless attitude of defeat.
When anyone considers the problem which civil defence authorities are supposed to be trying to deal with, it is not too difficult to see the reason for the confusion, the apathy and the frustration which seems to surround this subject in some areas of Canada; for civil defence, by its very nature, in this cold war period can have no fixed or accurate terms of reference. We are trying to build up some protection against a risk the nature of which has, through force of circumstances, very many unknowns. We do not know if an attack will take place. We do not know when an attack will take place, whether it will be a year from now, ten years from now or twenty years from now. We do not know what part of Canada is likely to be hit, or the nature of the weapons that are likely to be used, or the probable frequency or intensity of the attack.
When it comes to a consideration of the terrible new weapons which are likely to be used in any future war-the atom bomb and the hydrogen bomb-we have access only within limits and in rather secondhand fashion to such information as may be supplied to us by the military and scientific authorities of friendly countries.
We have little or no means of establishing the detailed nature of the problems that we have to face by resources which we have at our own disposal, and even the information which we obtain from other friendly sources is in a sense theoretical because in fact, with the exception of the atomic bombs which were dropped on Hiroshima and Nagasaki in 1945, no atomic or hydrogen weapon has ever been used on military forces or on the civilian population in any other part of the world. In view of these facts it is not surprising that military, scientific and civil defence authorities of this and other countries should find themselves in a position where they have not
The Address-Mr. Robertson yet all the answers to the question, how do we protect ourselves against the atom or hydrogen bomb?
I suspect that few members of the house and an even lower percentage of our general population have yet absorbed the full significance of the reports which have been published on the effect of the hydrogen bomb. Once the Canadian public learns the extent of this threat and the size of it, I am sure we will have an end to such incidents as we have witnessed in the cities of Victoria, Peterborough and Montreal. As you know, within the last year the civic authorities in these three centres have said they would discontinue their small civil defence organizations. I am happy to know, however, that on second thought the civic authorities in Victoria and Peterborough reconsidered this decision and are now carrying on their civil defence organizations in a much firmer way than before. I have reason to hope and I am confident that the civic authorities in the great city of Montreal, once they have had an opportunity to learn all the aspects of the problem, will reconsider their decision, and that we will see their civic defence organization established on an even firmer basis.
It is, I believe, the responsibility of each member of the house to support the development of a strong and alert civil defence organization in that part of Canada which he represents. In order to do so effectively it is necessary that each member have a clear understanding of the destructive power of the hydrogen bomb. I firmly believe that if we can get, on the part of all governments, a clearer understanding of what the hydrogen bomb can accomplish in the way of death and destruction, we will then have no more uncertainties and no more arguments as to whose responsibility it is to provide a civil defence set-up. This is not the time for provincial and local governments to think of withdrawing their support. No government can do this job alone, not even the federal government.
I am one who believes that responsibility for the survival of its own citizens is part of the responsibility of every form of government in Canada. It clearly requires the moral and financial support of every level of government in Canada and, more than that, it requires the participation not only of governments but of the citizens themselves.
I should like to give you now a few facts as to the destructive power and after-effects of hydrogen and atom bomb explosions, to illustrate the size of the potential danger which we must understand and communicate to the people whom we represent. My information comes in all cases from published sources, particularly the bulletin of atomic

The Address-Mr. Robertson scientists, the issues for November and December, 1954, and from a release on the effects of the hydrogen bomb issued by the United Kingdom home office and appearing in the British magazine Civil Defence.
In this last-mentioned magazine there is an interesting and awe-inspiring table giving the terrific increase in the destructive power of thermonuclear weapons since August 1945, when the first bombs were dropped on Hiroshima and Nagasaki. Those bombs are now known as nominal atomic bombs, and in their destructive power represented that of 20 kilo-tons of t.n.t., which is 20,000 tons of t.n.t. I do not believe that the general public has yet begun to appreciate the destructive powers even of the outmoded nominal atomic bomb of 1945. These bombs, carried in a single plane, encompassed as much destruction as was encompassed by our 1,000-plane raids over a number of German cities during the last great war.
We cannot really grasp even yet what it would mean if one of these bombs should be dropped on one of our Canadian cities. There would be an area of total destruction one mile in diameter in which every building and every individual would, in a single instant, be destroyed or killed. However, the nominal atomic bomb is now the water pistol of the thermonuclear age. Atomic bombs grew to 1,000 kilotons. They grew until we knew that there were atomic bombs of a striking force equal to one megaton or 1,000,000 tons of t.n.t.
The giant hydrogen bomb first appeared in the United States tests of 1952 and in the Russian tests of 1953, and then on a larger scale again in the early part of last year. It is reported by the magazine Civil Defence, to which I referred a few minutes ago, that the United States now possesses bombs of the nature of 20 megatons in strength. This means that one bomb has the striking force of 20 million tons of t.n.t., 1,000 times as strong as the nominal atomic bomb first used in 1945.
Let me refer again to Hiroshima and Nagasaki. A nominal atomic bomb was dropped killing some 45,000 people in one city and 25,000 in another, and producing an area of total destruction about one mile in diameter. Today we know that we have hydrogen bombs 1,000 times as powerful. How can we measure the destruction certain to be created if one of these bombs should be dropped? I turn again to the British home office article, and I read there that the area of total destruction would be a circular area some five miles in radius and 10 miles in diameter, within which everything would be totally destroyed. We know that the cities of

Hull and Ottawa could be encompassed in such an area. That means that if a bomb were dropped at ground level in this area the whole of metropolitan Ottawa and Hull would be destroyed.
But that is not all of this terrible story. Extending for another seven and a half miles in all directions would be an area of irreparable damage in which every building would be, for all useful purposes, destroyed, and most of the people in that area would be likewise killed or injured. Extending beyond that again for another seven and a half miles would be another area of extensive damage in which the buildings could possibly be repaired for future use.
I have described in some detail, Mr. Speaker, the area of destruction covered by this largest in the family of hydrogen weapons to date because I think it is important to impress upon the house and upon the people generally the large city and suburban areas which can be blasted into oblivion by the hydrogen bomb.
I have dealt principally with the blast effects of the hydrogen bomb, and have said nothing about the equally devastating effects of heat and fire. I do not propose to go into this phase of the subject because time will not permit. I should like to say, however, that Dr. Ralph E. Lapp, one of the United States' greatest atomic scientists, writing in the November issue of the bulletin for atomic scientists, in an article entitled "Civil defence faces new peril" said that the 10-megaton bomb-about one-half the size of the bomb to which I referred a minute ago-had a fireball measuring some three and one-quarter miles in diameter.
Anyone who has seen the film of the United States hydrogen bomb explosion of November 1952 entitled "Operation Ivy" can testify as to the awe-inspiring nature of the fireball resulting from that explosion. There was a mass of angry, seething, burning gases which literally consumed all the air and destroyed, in a single instant, everything that had not already been devastated by the explosive force in an area some three and a quarter miles in diameter. If you compared all the fires which would take place in Canada over the period of one year with the fireball resulting from this explosion, the fireball would dwarf the sum total of those fires.
But fire and blast are not the only deathdealing or destructive weapons resulting from the explosion of a hydrogen bomb. We have to deal with a new element, namely radioactivity. In the past we have had to deal with explosive and fire effects, but never on the same scale as we would have to deal

with them following the explosion of a hydrogen bomb. We have never, however, had to deal with the problem of radioactivity. If war should come this could very well be one of the problems facing civil defence workers in this country. Much has been said and written about the radiation that exists at the time of the bomb explosion. We know that then large quantities of alpha, gamma and beta rays are set free, and that unprotected persons exposed to these rays within a few miles of the point of explosion might be subject to lethal doses of radioactivity even though the time taken for this radioactive flash is only a relatively few seconds.
More serious than this, however, is the radioactive fall-out which takes place. Large quantities of debris and dust are sent upward into the mushroom cloud resulting from the explosion. They become impregnated with radioactive materials, and they are forced into the upper air by the nature of the explosion. This material is carried by the wind and may produce very serious damage in areas many miles from the point of explosion. We have all read of the serious illness which affected the fishermen on a Japanese fishing vessel, and the death of one of these fishermen, as a result of being subjected to this radioactive fall-out.
There is plenty of evidence coming out of the experience of these tests, and now appearing in published form, which suggests that not only the very large area directly affected by blast and fire as the result of an H-bomb explosion, but also a much larger area extending many miles downwind from the target city itself will be equally subjected to the danger of this lethal radioactive fall-out.
What does all this mean, Mr. Speaker, so far as civil defence is concerned? Clearly it means that the dimensions of the problem are greatly increased over what they were a year or two ago. When the bombs were dropping over the cities of England during world war II, it was possible to think in terms of standing fast and fighting it out. Dr. Ralph Lapp, in the article to which I have already referred, clearly indicates the existence of a new state of affairs when he says that distance is now the best defence against the bomb. What does this mean? It means surely that our best hope of saving lives in the event of an attack with atomic or hydrogen bombs is to take advantage of any advance warning we can get. We should plan to move as many people as possible out of the target area before the bomb lands. It has to be recognized that there is no hope whatever of survival for those people caught in even our largest cities at the moment the bomb is dropped. Their principal hope of survival lies 50433-41
The Address-Mr. Robertson in the possibility of getting several hours advance warning, and getting them away from the danger point. It is for that reason that civil defence in Canada is giving, and I believe should continue to give, attention to the possibilites of traffic control, planned evacuation of our cities and the development of ways and means by which people can be housed, fed and clothed in reception areas 50 or perhaps even 100 miles away from their normal place of abode. Experiments have shown that large cities can be evacuated in a relatively short time. If there is time after a strategic alert, evacuation can be on a gradual basis and only those people required to stay in the city would have to be removed on short notice. Wide exit lanes can be built out of our larger cities which would allow the swift removal of the people from them.
This problem is difficult and complicated indeed. It involves careful planning of the quickest and best means of getting large numbers of people moved rapidly out of our crowded urban areas. Each city will present its problems. Each city must have its own individual plan. Above all, the co-operation of the people themselves in remaining disciplined and obeying the instructions given them by their authorities during test exercises and on other occasions is essential to [DOT]the successful operation of such plans. Fortunately the expense of such a plan, of such an organization, of tests and practices designed to increase the efficiency of such an operation, need not be very great. Knowledge of local traffic conditions already exists on the local level. Municipal authorities already have, in their police and traffic forces, a nucleus on which to build an excellent plan for their own population. Much can be done with a well thought out plan based on detailed knowledge and supported by the local civic authorities as well as the population of the community itself.
It is clear that the number of people exposed to death and injury from hydrogen bombs is very great indeed, but it is also true that sound civil defence planning can possibly save more lives than ever before. Because of the wider areas of damage that are now possible, mutual aid among communities large and small takes on added importance. In certain localities mobile columns should be organized which could come to the assistance of neighbouring communities. Shelters located at the periphery of target areas would provide some measure of protection to people who must remain there. Radioactivity can kill people many miles removed from the explosion centre, but shelters that would provide an earth cover of three feet would give a great measure of

The Address-Mr. Bourque protection against radioactive fall-out. High intensity radiation meters and people trained in their use would be invaluable to indicate when it is safe for people to leave their shelters. Inhalation or ingestion of radioactive debris is a matter that requires further study, but there is much hope that proper respirators can afford great protection against inhalation of these poisonous substances.
Plant location is another matter which should be considered in the light of our present knowledge of hydrogen bomb warfare, in order that our ability to wage war should not be impaired by the destruction of our industrial capacity and the death of our industrial workers.
I do not suggest that civil defence has reduced itself to this single, simple formula. That is far from being the case. We have, of course, to contemplate the possibility that other kinds of weapons besides the H-bomb may be used, and for these alternative possibilities we must continue to carry out the kind of civil defence operation and organization that we have been accustomed to in the past. We cannot discontinue our training in the fields of fire fighting and rescue training; we cannot discontinue our planning in the medical field. We will certainly under any conceivable form of attack need a sound system of warning and communications.
All these are elements in our present program of training and preparation. All these will be needed under the new circumstances which have developed out of the hydrogen bomb tests of the last few years. But what has emerged more clearly than anything else is that in terms of the use of these largest weapons of destruction only those who prepare their plans ahead of time, only those who remain disciplined and calm and cooperate with the proper authorities in removing themselves from the point of danger as far as possible in advance of the actual incident, can have any hope of survival. It is well for us to recognize this now, because only by recognizing it and co-operating at all levels of government to bring the importance of these facts home to the people can we begin to think through the kind of constructive civil defence plan and program which will be just as essential for our survival as the armed forces themselves.

Mr. Speaker, may I be permitted, at the beginning of this speech, to add my congratulations to those extended by previous speakers to the mover (Mr. Leduc) and seconder (Mr. Carrick) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne, for the ease with which they

both carried out their task. I am sure they will leave their mark in this house and that their voice will add to the interest of the debates in which they will take part.
(Text):
Mr. Speaker, the comments made by some of the opposition members who have spoken in this debate have sometimes ranged far from the subject under discussion, which may be the natural result of their finding little or nothing to criticize. The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Regier), for instance, gave us an interesting summary of the opinions he formed of his fellow Canadians following a trip across Canada last fall.
I agree with him that we would all benefit by adding to our knowledge of our own country by visiting each of our ten provinces, and that is an opportunity which I am sure each one of us would be happy to grasp.
Like the hon. member from British Columbia I too have been pleased to travel across this dominion. Just two years ago I visited his home province for the first time, and I was greatly impressed by all I saw there. I found the people of British Columbia extremely kind and hospitable. As a French Canadian I was received with the warmest kindness. While I was able to spend only a few days in Vancouver, I must confess that I found there no disturbing signs which would indicate any immediate danger of an outbreak of communism or of any other "ism" which would imperil our country. I found British Columbians to be much the same as Canadians in every other province I have visited, very much the same as the people I meet and see in Montreal or Quebec city.
However, the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam had an entirely different experience in the province of Quebec. It makes me wonder who were the people he met during his sojourn there. Historically the province of Quebec has always been an honest, industrious and God-fearing province. Rich in natural resources, it is equally rich in the quality of its people. It enjoys to a greater degree than any other province, with the possible exception of New Brunswick-the state of which the hon. member also found disturbing-the benefit of two great cultures, French and Anglo-Saxon. More than any other, too, it has found out how to blend these two cultures so that instead of being antagonistic to each other they are complementary.
Quebec, too, is prosperous. Possessor of more than 50 per cent of Canada's developed water power, it is home to many of this country's greatest industries. Capital from many parts of the world, as well as from other parts of Canada, has found a safe field for

investment in Quebec, and millions of tourists each year come to visit that oldest section of Canada.
This surely is not the background for a communist revolution. Nor could the great majority of Quebec people, who are faithful adherents of the Catholic church, be considered likely recruits for the godless forces of international communism. Throughout the world the Catholic church is recognized as the great bulwark against the red peril, and in Quebec its members are not all French-speaking. It is the church of people of many races, loyally supported by Canadians of many different origins.
A province so wealthy, so long noted for its industry and thrift, so successful in promoting harmony and happiness among its people of differing languages and culture, is not a very logical hunting ground for the sowers of hatred and discord. I am surprised that the hon. member found among our many hundreds of thousands of loyal and contented citizens the few who would seek to foment trouble even if they lived in paradise.
When he refers to the fact that the communists in Montreal polled more votes than the C.C.F. party to which he belongs, the hon. member, I am afraid, was not pointing up the menace of communism as much as he was demonstrating the failure of his own brand of socialism, which has not yet succeeded in electing a single member from the province of Quebec.
At the conclusion of this session the hon. member might be well advised to spend more time in his own constituency, where the voters have already taken the first step in the direction which the member fears and have moved away from the political parties which gave this country birth and have brought it to its present stage of development. There he is more likely to find the measure of his discontent.
Mr. Speaker, I was very pleased to read in the Financial Times, issue of January 21, 1955, the statement of Mr. H. D. Scott, superintendent of foreign business for the Imperial Bank of Canada, who has just returned from a three months, 40,000 mile trip, which took him to Australia, New Zealand, Japan, India and Pakistan, as well as the United Kingdom. He said:
"Canada's record has never stood higher in the estimation of foreign countries than at the present time", he said, "and Canada's trade and diplomatic officers were doing an exceptionally fine job wherever I met them. These government officers working overseas are a tremendous help to the Canadian businessman visiting foreign countries.
X cannot speak too highly of their help and service.
"Canada is greatly respected throughout the free world", Mr. Scott said, "and there is absolutely no doubt that countries in the Far East and in the
50433-41J
The Address-Mr. Bourque western hemisphere admire the manner in which we have conducted our economy during the postwar years and are amazed at our industrial and business development. Wherever I went I was told that Canada is truly a remarkable country."
To return to the outline of the legislation contained in the speech from the throne, I should like to refer briefly to two specific items. The first is the amendments which are to be made to the Blind Persons Act; the second is this government's support of the rearmament of Germany. To the first I give my wholehearted support. The second I support, as I suppose many of us do, as the lesser of two evils. I fear it, but I see no alternative.
The hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Cavers) expressed the hope that a greater measure of help will be given to the blind, and referred to those in his constituency who suffer from this great affliction. For many years I have been keenly interested in the welfare of the blind in the province of Quebec, and have been an active supporter of the Canadian National Institute for the Blind. My work with these people has been one of the most inspiring and most heart-warming experiences of my life. I have visited and talked and worked with many who live in a world of perpetual darkness. Seldom if ever have I heard a word of complaint. I have heard of their difficulties in making a living, and of how they have overcome those difficulties. I have heard, too, of the petty criminals who take advantage of blind people in the course of their day to day business.
These people deserve all the help that can>
be given them, because they do not depend upon help but are eager to serve themselves. Any more generous provision for their care and assistance that this government can give them will, I am sure, be warmly supported from all sides of the house. This is not a political matter; it is a humanitarian action which we all approve.
The question of rearming Germany is an entirely different thing. Just as many of us during our lives have come in contact with the blind, so have many of us seen the horrors of war which have been visited upon us twice during a quarter of a century. We know personally the victims of German oppression and German atrocities. We recall all too clearly the days of the 1930's when a rearming Germany once more became the scourge of the world. For six years we fought a rearmed Germany in defence of freedom and human decency. As we laid down our arms we hoped fervently that we would never be called upon to pick them up again, and in our wisdom we decided that the power to destroy should never again be restored to Germany's bloodstained hands.

The Address-Mr. Bourque
Just a few days ago I was reading in my copy of Hansard for April 17, 1951, the maiden speech in this house by the hon. member for Cartier (Mr. Crestohl). He declared, in much stronger terms than I could, his opposition to any move which would result in the rearming of Germany. "We are now considering," he said, "placing weapons in their hands once more. What can we expect in 1952, 1953, 1954 and the years that will follow?" he asked.
Well, the years 1952, 1953 and 1954 have come and gone, and the great German problem which the hon. member for Cartier feared at that time has given way to an even greater problem. How can we defend our freedom and our democracy against the menace to the east without the aid of our former enemy? History does not always permit us to be logical and almost never permits us to be sentimental. England fought for many long years against the tyranny of Napoleon. No greater enmity in the world existed than that between England and France. Yet in the face of new perils the two nations became allies and, even more important, friends.
Had Britain determined that her ancient enemy, France, should be forever disarmed, who would have stood by Britain's side against the Hun in 1914-1918? Then there might not even have been a second world war in which France, weak as she was, would once more face the German horde and give Britain at least a little time to prepare her defence.
We who have lived through two great wars can have little love for Germany and little desire to restore her might. But we must live with history; we must realize that selfpreservation is sometimes more important than sentiment, and that allies cannot always be chosen for reasons of affection. During the war we had the Soviet union as an ally, though many of us accepted her with grave doubts. Even Sir Winston Churchill, Britain's wartime Prime Minister, greeted this unexpected and new-found friend with considerable lack of enthusiasm. "I will accept aid from wherever it comes", he said, "satisfied that Germans killed by Russians would be just as successfully removed from the war as Germans killed by Englishmen or Canadians or anyone else."
Today I am pleased to see that the hon. member for Cartier, realizing that conditions existing in 1955 are different, like all of us has put aside his personal emotions and decided to accept the lesser of two evils. I am sure he agrees that we are in much the same historical position. West Germany is necessary to our defence, necessary perhaps to our survival.

Represented as we are in the councils of Europe by our able Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) we receive our information at first hand. We have no experience in foreign intrigues, and we want none. We are prepared to face facts, however distasteful they may be, and the facts as presented to us by the Secretary of State for External Affairs indicate that as members of the western community, as defenders of western ideals, we will be better served if we approve this rearmament policy than if we oppose it.
My support of this policy, I must admit, has been strengthened by the volume of mail and the number of petitions that have reached my desk in opposition to it. The communist friends of Soviet Russia in this country are against rearming West Germany. They are doing everything they can to prevent it. They have succeeded in convincing me even, I must say, against my wishes, that it is our only salvation.

speechtext:
In these perilous times, the speech from the throne delivered to this parliament revealed much for which we can be thankful. We are far removed from the immediate and devastating threats of war. We are enjoying a prosperity which is built upon sound foundations. Even some of our good Tory newspapers do not hesitate, from time to time, to report news which tells us how fortunate we are to live under this good Liberal administration.
Arthur Blakely, parliamentary correspondent for the Conservative Montreal Gazette, reported in his column on January 13:
Canadian housewives, irritated by high coffee prices, would be more so if they were on the other side of the curtain. A pound of coffee goes for the equivalent of $4.78 in Russia. The Rumanian price tag is even higher, $6.47. Further west, in Hungary, the price is $13.54 per pound. And in coffee-loving Czechoslovakia, it is $18.85. Poland, reports here indicate, places the highest price tag of all on coffee. The asking price: $45.45 per pound.

In Canada prices have remained at reasonable levels and earnings have been reasonably high. The proof is to be found in the possessions of the average Canadian family acquired since the war. More people own their own homes, drive their own cars, have television sets, radios and even record players than ever before. More students are enrolled in our colleges and universities. More people of all ages crowd our winter and summer resorts and go to our moving picture theatres and sports events.
Opposition members have made much of the reports of increased unemployment, but unemployment is not cured by unemployment insurance or even by public works which, necessary to a degree, are an important part of government policy.
The amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act reveal the government's acceptance of its responsibility for those who are without work. They provide an increase in unemployment benefits from $2.15 to $2.85 a day in the case of a person without dependents, and from $2.80 to $4.00 a day in the case of a person with dependents. This involves a maximum daily contribution of
9	cents for the insured person. At present a person in class 2 who has the minimum number of qualifying contributions, namely 90, is entitled to 16 days' benefits. The amendment increases this minimum to 60 days or
10 weeks, and will not affect those who qualify for more.
This provision will allow every recipient in the supplementary benefit period of 1955 to benefit for the minimum period of 60 days, and if they have exhausted their entitlement they will receive the difference between the number of days already obtained and the 60-day guarantee. A review of the situation as it exists in Canada today will, I believe, satisfy any hon. member that this phase of government policy is fair and reasonable. But the real remedy lies in hard work, increased production and sound business. It is those qualities which this government seeks to encourage and promote, and I wholeheartedly support those policies designed to create a climate in which the economy of this nation can successfully operate.
Many serious problems will face hon. members during this session and in future sessions. I believe we are all prepared to give these problems serious, fair and honest consideration. To those who criticize us for increasing our salary to $10,000 a year I would refer to a recent newspaper heading: "Bob Hope Gets $100,000 as M.C. for T.V. Hour," or to the newspaper reports which carried the story that Jackie Gleason, an
The Address-Mr. Stanton American comedian, signed a three-year T.V. contract for $7 million per year. Surely, by comparison, we in this house are not overpaid.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak in the throne speech debate I would like to congratulate the hon. members for Verdun (Mr. Leduc) and Trinity (Mr. Carrick) on the able manner in which they moved and seconded the address in reply to the speech from the throne. They did an excellent job, particularly when we consider the small amount of material with which they had to work. I am sure they did their best to make a lot out of a little.
They and other Liberal speakers have tried to make the people of Canada believe that milk and honey flow from this Liberal government, but if that is the case I would suggest to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) that he extend that pipeline across Canada as speedily as possible, so that some of that milk and honey will flow into the homes of those who are unemployed in this country at the present time.
The government, we are pleased to note, has at long last reviewed the plight of many of our war veterans, and is considering ways and means of relieving their burdens. This is exactly what the different Legion branches across Canada have been urging. We must realize and admit that the members of that body of service men and women have never been, nor are they now, unreasonable in their demands. The legislation they asked for last session received favourable consideration from the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Lapointe) but somewhere, somehow, after the presentation of their brief to the minister, something went wrong within the cabinet and they did not receive the support that was justly theirs.
In formulating legislation for veterans and blind pensioners, the government seems inclined to place them in the same category as those receiving old age assistance. This should not be. I believe that when we are considering the welfare of our returned men and women we should throw aside any hint of party politics and consider every request from the dominion command of the Legion, and all legislation pertaining to their welfare, strictly on its merits, to give them whatever benefits we can which will contribute to making brighter the lives of those who are maimed, or who are discouraged by adversity in the sunset of life. They have it coming to them and I hope the government, now that it has announced consideration of the veterans' request, will not do as it did in 1954 and forget about them before the session closes.

The Address-Mr. Stanton
Nearly every item that has been mentioned in the address has been suggested or sponsored by members of the opposition in the last few sessions. The government are past masters in the art of availing themselves of constructive legislation based on suggestions of opposition members. They were prodded all last session for additional benefits for the disabled men and women of the army, navy and air force; they have been prodded for more generous treatment to the blind. No doubt they would never have thought of either of these matters if it had not been for the opposition members bringing this much-needed social legislation to the attention of the house.
Now that consideration, which is long overdue, is being given to the extent of $5 million for the removal of hazardous railway crossings, which are taking a greater toll of human life every year, I hope the expenditure will be distributed evenly across Canada where it is most needed, and not where political pressure is greatest.
I must at this point deviate from my address in order to bring to the attention of the government, and especially of the departments concerned, a situation that exists at Brock-ville. Trains that stop at this station cut across the main avenue from the north, which consists of highways No. 42 and No. 29. This is not only inconvenient because long lines of traffic are held up for long intervals; it is also dangerous, as two schools are now situated north of the tracks. Neither Brockville nor any other place can afford to lose even one of its children. I am sure the people of this county town would greatly appreciate a subway or overhead pass to take care of the ever-increasing traffic.
I was much amused to read in some of the old Hansard reports the remark made by the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) to the effect that the old station in his constituency had bedbugs, and that a new one was needed. Our station at Brockville has not yet reached that stage, but it is far from adequate for a thriving town and community of nearly 20,000 people; it is more suitable for a small town or village.
There are three major improvements that the town of Brockville must have if it is to keep its place in the expansion of eastern Ontario. The first is a subway or overpass at the northern limits of the town. This is a necessity at the present time. The second is a more modern station to take care of the ever-increasing population which the building and completion of the St. Lawrence seaway will bring. Third, and perhaps most important, is dockage that will be adequate to

accommodate the freighters that will be plying the St. Lawrence and the great lakes when this project is completed.
I cannot be unmindful of the unemployment which exists at the present time, and which is growing week by week. I shall not take time to deal with its many complexities. That has already been done by other members of this party. However, I should like to draw the attention of the house to the situation in which the employees of our two railways find themselves. In the early part of January of this year it was announced that 50 men would be laid off from the division between Cornwall and Gananoque. This is only what is happening to the railway employees all across Canada. The minister has admitted these lay-offs, and still the government is not putting forth any effort to effect a remedy but rather is sitting smug in the knowledge of its large majority. Many of these railway-men have their homes in communities in which they have always lived, and it is not easy for them to pull up at a moment's notice and move to a place unknown to them.
You may ask what is the remedy. There are few ills for which there is no remedy. In 1934 the then minister of public works had inserted in all departmental contracts a clause which read as follows:
Transportation of material and plant: All material and plant used in connection with the execution of this contract must be transported over railways operating in Canada to the greatest possible extent.
The Department of Transport construction contract forms contained a similar clause. Recently the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Winters) and the former minister of transport caused the deletion of this clause from their contracts. Surely this clause, which has served such a useful purpose through all these years, could still serve in diverting to the railways much valuable traffic which they formerly enjoyed. Surely the government should be anxious to divert as much traffic as possible and as large a volume of business as possible through the channels of its own railroad.
We must realize that the railroads must work under many restrictions and conform to many regulations laid down by the board of transport commissioners, who have no jurisdiction over international and interprovincial highway operations. Although the supreme court and recently the privy council held that the federal authorities had jurisdiction over these highway operations, the government has lamely taken steps to hand these powers over to the provinces. So often when there is a decision to be made on some controversial question the government backs

away, meekly says "This is not our baby", and immediately tosses it over to the provinces. It is an old habit of the government when it does not want to face up to an issue.
Representing as I do a constituency that is 50 per cent rural, I would be remiss in my duty-indeed, I would feel myself to be a poor representative of that grand old riding of Leeds which produces an abundance of milk and milk products, especially cheese- if I did not at this time bring to the attention of the government the situation in which the producers find themselves at the present time. This situation will become far more acute as time goes on if New Zealand cheese continues to be imported into Canada.
It is an impossibility for Canadian dairy farmers to compete against their neighbours in the southern hemisphere in the matter of producing milk and milk products. We must realize that in Canada, on the average 100 acre dairy farm, the capital expenditure for buildings in which to house the cattle in the winter and for implements to produce food for those cattle for nearly seven months of the year, is at least $15,000. Furthermore, it will take one man to care for and to produce the feed for the winter months on a farm that will accommodate 15 dairy cows; and if he works only eight hours a day, or 40 hours a week, that number of cows will be materially decreased. How then can the Minister of Trade and Commerce or the government expect the dairy industry here, under these conditions, to compete with the dairymen of New Zealand who do not have to provide winter accommodation for their cattle, except a milking shed; where they do not have to provide any winter feed because the cattle have the advantage of pasture the year round; and where each farmer, by not having to provide winter care or feed, is able to milk and care for an average herd of 40 to 50 dairy cows? Again I say it is impossible for a dairy farmer in Canada to produce milk and milk products on a competitive basis with New Zealand. It just cannot be done.
While high tariffs and import quotas are unwise, perhaps, in the long run, Canadian industry is protected by substantial tariffs- and perhaps rightly so-running in many cases from 20 to 35 per cent and as high as 40 per cent. At the time the Minister of Trade and Commerce offers to balance New Zealand's trade budget by taking 2J million pounds of cheese, Canadian farm products are shut out of many world markets by embargoes. New Zealand has carefully restricted imports since 1938, yet our government is allowing cheese to come into Canada after the Ontario cheese producers have contributed
The Address-Mr. Stanton over $1 million of their own money to stabilize cheese prices and permit them to offer a more acceptable and attractive price to the importers of Great Britain. The government apparently has no constructive trade policy regarding farm products, more especially with Great Britain which has always been our most stable market. Now we have 2J million pounds of imported cheese, and no assurance from the minister that there will not be more. He has intimated to the house that he does not expect any more for six or nine months. I suppose he thinks that by that time the farmers will have forgotten.
I consider this is a real slap in the face to the dairymen of the dominion. It hits at the very economy of our agricultural industry, in which dairying plays so important a part. When the purchasing power of the rural district is lowered, the economy of the whole country suffers. No truer words were ever spoken than those of that celebrated finance minister, Sir Thomas White, when he stated that the economy and prosperity of a nation lie in the top six inches of soil.
Farm incomes have been materially reduced during 1953 and 1954, and the effects are already being felt across Canada. There is not at the present time the purchasing power there was some three years ago, and as a consequence there has been a serious unemployment situation at the Cockshutt plant at Brantford and the Massey-Harris works at Toronto. Worst of all, that grand old firm of Frost and Wood, later a subsidiary of Cockshutt, which has been the backbone of Smiths Falls through all these years, I believe since 1892, has ceased to operate on account of decreased sales. This will be a serious blow to the employees, many of whom are past middle life and have established homes for themselves and their families.
Agriculture, I contend-and I want to bring this to the attention of hon. members-should be thrifty enough and have an income sufficient to be able to compete with urban industry in wages. By so doing it would supply employment instead of furnishing employees for the urban centres. There are thousands of cars and buses commuting daily from the rural districts to the larger towns and cities. Why do they do this? It is only natural that people go where the remuneration for their labour is highest. Therefore it is plain to be seen that if the agriculturists of this dominion-and you will take notice that I use the word "dominion"-were able to compete in the wage field this labour trend would not be so pronounced. Indeed, I believe it would not be half what it is at the present time. It is simple mathematics. If there are not enough jobs for all, then for

The Address-Mr. Stanton every 100 men who commute to work from the rural areas there will be 100 unemployed in the town or city.
Knowing that New Zealand cheese will soon be on sale in our grocery stores, it is indeed hard for me to take part in the debate regarding this situation without using words most unbecoming to the dignity of the house. I wonder what the Minister of Agriculture would have said if 2J million bushels of wheat had been dumped into Canada from the Argentine, Australia or some other wheat-producing country. I wonder what the hon. members on my left, the socialists, would have said if their wheat market hung in the balance. I am sure they would have protested so loudly, and rightly so, that the sound barriers of this house would have been broken.
I cannot understand how so many hon. members on the government side of the house who represent dairying constituencies can be so patient at this time when the economy of their people is threatened. They must be a well disciplined group, quite content with the decision of their superiors even if it does distress and make the going more difficult for their people. That is what the present government is doing, making it as impossible as it can for the dairy farmer. However, I must congratulate the hon. member for Glengarry-Prescott (Mr. Bruneau) for his outspoken address on the subject that is uppermost in the minds of his people at the present time. He and the hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Viau) must have more courage than their associates.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce, by stating that he did not think there would be any more shipments of New Zealand cheese for the next six or nine months, has created a very uncertain and shrouded situation for the coming year. The Ontario cheese marketing board, the cheese producers' association and the farmers who produce that commodity do not know at the present time just where they are at.
I hold in my hand a portion of Canadian cheddar, which is not one of the finest but the finest and most appetizing cheese to be found in any country. It is a crying shame that we have to be subjected to the importation of an inferior quality of cheese when we have in storage now over 41 million pounds with a surplus of nearly 12 million pounds for which we have no market at the present time.
I should like to draw to the attention of the house and the people of Canada just what this shipment of New Zealand cheese means in pounds of milk. An amount of 2,250,000 pounds of cheese is equivalent to 28,125,000 pounds of milk or, to break it down again, is equal to the yearly production of 3,515


average dairy cows. We may then readily understand that the importation of this cheese means that hundreds of Canadian farmers will have decreased incomes.
I hope the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Agriculture, who gave the previous shipment of New Zealand cheese his blessing and who should be near the people whom he represents so far as their problems are concerned, will give to the house and to the dairy farmers of Canada some definite statement as to the importation of cheese. I am sure that any future shipments can be suspended by embargoes or import quotas which the government has the authority to impose, as it did in the case of Japanese shirts and many other articles that were about to come into the country, or by higher tariffs which give adequate protection to many of our other industries.
Why let one of our major industries suffer while others benefit? If there are any future importations of New Zealand cheese while we have such large surpluses of this product as we have at the present time-and cheese is the most logical way of disposing of our surplus milk-I hope the menu of the two hon. ministers will consist of nothing more than limburger cheese, and I am sure that all the cheese producers join with me in this wish.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to begin by congratulating the mover (Mr. Leduc) and the seconder (Mr. Carrick) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. It is also a pleasure to congratulate the new members and the new ministers. I offer them my best wishes.
(Text):
I should like to take a few moments, Mr. Speaker, to outline some of the needs of the riding which I have the honour to represent in this house, and to inform the house of the feelings and opinions of the majority of my constituents in regard to certain questions relating to our national policy. Indeed, I deem it the duty of a member of parliament to devote himself, first of all, to the general interest of his country in accordance with the principles advocated by the political party under whose banner he was elected in his constituency, to inform the house when possible of the opinions of the majority of his constituents on the various topics of current interest, and to acquaint the government with certain legitimate needs in his constituency.
The riding of Dollard may be subdivided into two sections. Ville St. Laurent, located northwest of the city of Montreal, and the northeastern part of Montreal, which extends from Guizot and Fleury streets to the limits of Ville St. Michel. In the last few years a tremendous development has taken place in these two sections of Dollard. The population has doubled, many new parishes have been organized, and hundreds of new industries large and small have established themselves there. In the circumstances it is readily understood that the needs of the population have increased. I could describe the riding of Dollard in detail and speak of its 50433-42
The Address-Mr. Rouleau greatness and beauty, but I need not do so. All I have to say is that to me it is a good place, a beautiful and progressive district. In short, it is a great place to live because it is part of Canada, and it is the part of Canada that I have the honour to represent in this house.
I said, Mr. Speaker, that I was going to stress some of the needs of my riding. There is one need resulting from the railroad track which crosses the constituency from end to end. The constituency of Dollard is crossed by several railways. These tracks provide a great service to the population and to industry, not only of the riding of Dollard but the island of Montreal as a whole. On the other hand they greatly inconvenience the residents of my riding. In the section of Montreal which is included in Dollard riding the railway track is elevated, thus dividing it into two parts in so far as road traffic is concerned. In order to facilitate north-south traffic it has been necessary to build subways under these railway tracks to allow the traffic to flow through the main arteries of Montreal.
Most of the important arteries are open to traffic, but with the rapid development which has taken place it is urgent that others be opened, and more particularly De Lorimier street. Before long this street will be one of Montreal's most important thoroughfares, crossing the island from north to south. There is already a temporary subway at that point, but it is too narrow and dangerous. It should be enlarged immediately and finished permanently.
Another problem raised by these elevated tracks is the smoke-belching steam locomotives passing thereon. The section of the city which this elevated track crosses is strictly a residential district, occupied by families who have built beautiful homes. When this railway was built a few years ago the residents understood that nothing but diesel or electric locomotives would be used. To that end the Canadian National had the necessary trolley wires installed when the line was constructed. However, the Canadian National, despite repeated representations by the citizens of Montreal North, and by members of this house who preceded me, persists all too often in routing steam locomotives over this track. These locomotives belch smoke and soot, making the whole district dirty and being harmful to the health of the citizens.
Irrespective of any promises which the Canadian National may have made, I strongly protest against what in my opinion constitutes an abuse, because the smoke coming from these locomotives not only prevents the residents from keeping their properties

The Address-Mr. Rouleau as clean as they would like but is also injurious to the children's health. In the name of my fellow citizens of Dollard I urgently request the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marler), the board of transport commissioners and the Canadian National to take the necessary steps to put an end to this practice. As the member for Dollard I shall not rest until justice has been done the families who live along these tracks.
In Ville St. Laurent the railway tracks are at ground level, which causes great inconvenience and constant danger to the population because of the numerous level crossings. I was pleased to note that according to the speech from the throne the government proposes to amend the Railway Act in connection with the elimination of level crossings, in order to implement the report of the board of transport commissioners in that respect. I am hopeful that in the course of the next few months it may be possible to eliminate several crossings in Ville St. Laurent, and also to provide protection in other cases.
During the course of last session the Ville St. Laurent council sent a delegation to Ottawa to present to the then minister of transport, Hon. Lionel Chevrier, a memorandum listing all the reasons in favour of building a subway on Decarie boulevard. This thoroughfare is the one most often used by Montrealers bound for the Laurentians. Because of increased railway traffic at this point not only has the ordinary traffic been slowed down, but a situation has developed which constitutes a very real danger in emergencies. In case of fire, for instance, the firemen would be delayed in getting to their destination. In case of accident the same considerations would apply to ambulances having to go over level crossings.
In the past these conditions have been the cause of catastrophies, to avoid a repetition of which it is urgent that action be taken on the just request of the Ville St. Laurent council. When the representatives of Ville St. Laurent met the minister of transport they were most graciously received and assured by the minister that he would do everything to grant their request. I take the liberty of submitting this question anew to the present Minister of Transport (Mr. Marler) who, I am sure, understands the problem perfectly and will do everything in his power to remedy the situation as soon as possible.
I would point out to the Minister of Transport also that adequate protection is urgently needed on Cote Vertu, O'Brien boulevard and Persillier boulevard. During the last few months we have been grieved by several fatal accidents at those level crossings.

(Translation):
We have not looked upon these accidents with equanimity, Mr. Speaker. We took the matter up with the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marler) who understands the problem. And we went to the board of transport commissioners, at the request of the municipal council of Ville St. Laurent, which is quite ready to help solve the problem.
The Minister of Transport understands the situation and the board of transport commissioners is ready to correct this anomaly as soon as possible.
I can appreciate the request made by the municipal council of Ville St. Laurent and bodies of its citizens, as well as the publicity given to this question by the newspapers of my constituency, such as the Saint-Laurent News. There is no one that does not wish to prevent a recurrence of the tragedies that have occurred within the last few months. Again, yesterday evening, a man was killed at the level crossing at Cote Vertu.
I offer my most sincere sympathy to the family of Mr. Adrien Lamarre, aged 36. I express the wholehearted wish that this situation may be corrected as quickly as possible. As far as I am concerned, I will take all steps necessary to prevent a recurrence of these tragedies. A human life is worth more than the money necessary for its protection.
(Text):
During the summer months the Postmaster General (Mr. Cote) honoured us by being present at the inauguration in the eastern part of Montreal of a new postal station at Youville, the construction of which had become necessary because of the rapid development in the area mentioned earlier. This is a very modern building which will be most useful to the population and for which I extend my most sincere thanks to the minister, to the officers of his department and to the Department of Public Works.
There is need for the same kind of building in Ville St. Laurent. The postal substation here was built at the turn of the century, when Ville St. Laurent was nothing but a village of a few thousand people. In 1947 there were 10,000 people in Ville St. Laurent, while today there are 40,000. Several hundred new industries have moved there.
Trade is keeping pace with industry and as a consequence the present substation is inadequate. Notwithstanding all their efforts the post office officials are unable under existing conditions to give the population and the industries satisfactory service. It is not only necessary, it is most urgent that a new postal station be built if the population are to be provided with the postal services to which they are entitled.

The Postmaster General and the officials of his department know the situation. At this time I should like to thank the minister, who was kind enough last summer to come with some of his officials to see what the situation was at this station. I am aware that the Postmaster General, along with his officials and the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Winters), is trying at the present time to work out a solution for the problem. On behalf of the citizens of Ville St. Laurent I wish to thank him.
Ville St. Laurent is privileged to have within its borders an airport of which it is proud. However, this airport which is located entirely within the limits of Ville St. Laurent is called Cartierville airport. The authorities of Ville St. Laurent have asked me, and I am in complete agreement with them, to submit to the Minister of Transport and to the board of transport commissioners that it would be logical for this airport to be known as St. Laurent airport. I take pleasure in submitting this request to the Minister of Transport, and I hope he will see his way clear to make the appropriate change. In addition to meeting the request of the authorities of Ville St. Laurent, I submit that it would honour the great Canadian who is the Prime Minister of Canada.
Such are some of the needs of Dollard riding. I hope the government will give them the consideration they deserve.
During the parliamentary recess I had the good fortune of meeting many of my constituents, and I would like to pass on to the house some of the opinions expressed to me and which seem to represent the wishes of the majority on a few questions of current interest.
My fellow citizens were gratified at the government's decision to locate the national film board in Dollard riding, and are pleased to see that a building is going up which will soon house its services. On their behalf I wish to thank the government and especially the Minister of Public Works, who is responsible for its construction.
It is also a matter of satisfaction to us that work on the St. Lawrence seaway has begun, convinced as we are that once the waterway is completed the whole country will benefit by it. However, I would support the authorities of the city of Montreal in their request to the government and to the St. Lawrence seaway authority to take the necessary steps to see that the interests of the city of Montreal, the metropolis of Canada, are protected.
As Canadians we are rightly proud of our metropolis, and it is our duty to ensure that the construction of the seaway will not hinder 50433-42J
The Address-Mr. Rouleau the development of Montreal, or cause it to lose its place as the metropolis of Canada. Many of my fellow citizens are concerned about this question; this is why I take the liberty of drawing the attention of this house and of the government to this matter, expressing the wish that in the development of the St. Lawrence seaway the interests of our metropolis will be considered as well as those of the whole of Canada. We shall be very happy if this new achievement, while being of great benefit to Canada at large, gives commercial impetus to the city of Montreal.
During the parliamentary recess I was often asked another question with regard to restrictions imposed by the board of governors of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation on privately-owned radio and television stations. Most of my fellow citizens whom I have met, not only in Dollard riding but also in Montreal and elsewhere in Canada, are opposed to the fact that this organization which competes directly with private enterprise should be at the same time the organization that controls and grants permits to private stations.
We know that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation through its radio and television networks renders a great service to our country, but we would prefer that it be treated on an equal footing, or nearly so, with stations belonging to private enterprise. Such a practice would be more consistent with the democratic principles of Liberalism, and furthermore it would comply with the resolutions passed by the advisory council of the national Liberal federation at its meeting held in Ottawa on the 27th and 28th of October, 1952. and also by the federation of young Liberals of Canada during their biannual convention held in May, 1954.
Before resuming my seat I wish on behalf of my fellow citizens of Dollard to thank the Prime Minister of Canada for everything he has done and continues to do to prevent an important group of our fellow citizens from being taxed more heavily than others. We are grateful to the Prime Minister for giving his attention to the problem of double taxation which exists in the province of Quebec, and I take this opportunity to protest vigorously against the astounding statement made on January 12 last by an hon. member of this house to the effect that the Prime Minister of Canada had lowered himself in going to meet the premier of my province in an effort to find a way of settling the fiscal problems between Quebec and Ottawa.
652	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Rouleau
Judging from his speech I am strongly under the impression that my hon. friend has some difficulty in understanding the facts and conditions that exist in his own country. This is why, lest he should misinterpret my words as he has misinterpreted the happenings in his own country and especially in the province of Quebec, I shall direct my remarks particularly to him and I shall speak in my mother tongue. He will have the opportunity, if he so wishes, to read them in the official translation of the debates of the house.
{Translation):
I will say to the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Regier) that, as a Canadian citizen and as a Liberal, I did not feel humiliated in seeing the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. St. Laurent) go to Montreal to meet the premier of one of the oldest provinces of my country, in order to find in a friendly atmosphere a solution to the problem existing between Quebec and Ottawa.
The Prime Minister of my country thus showed once more that he can raise himself above party politics when the welfare of the Canadian people is at stake.
With all the inhabitants of the province of Quebec, I read with a sigh of relief the report released by these two heads of governments following their meeting in Montreal, which allowed us to expect that the dispute which had lasted too long would be settled. By his unfortunate speech, the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam obviously showed that he lacks the broadmindedness required to fill a responsible position.
After a brief journey through the various provinces of our country, he found nothing better to do than to attack each one of the provinces which form the Canadian confederation, including the province where he lives. As far as I am concerned, I had the advantage to travel from coast to coast on three different occasions and, since he mentioned in his speech that he spent more days in the province of Quebec than six French-speaking members have spent so far in his own province, I would say to him that I had the pleasure of spending many weeks in the magnificent province of British Columbia and in the marvellous city of Vancouver. In every province of my country, I always found a cordial welcome and on my return to Montreal, I was always pleased and charmed with my fellow citizens and dazzled by the beauty and wealth of my country.
The hon. member could do no better than to find fault with each one of the provinces of confederation and it was with a vio-


lence full of hatred that he attacked the province of my birth. To dare predict that my province would be the first to turn communist, he must understand very little the feelings of its inhabitants or he must have met the rare exceptions who share his ideas. When he made his accusation, it struck me as so absurd that for a moment I wondered what was the reason for his attack and what he meant to achieve.
If there is in the Canadian confederation a province that is against communism it is indeed the province of Quebec; I am convinced that in this respect it shares the common feeling of the vast majority of the Canadian people. In describing his trip, the member for Burnaby-Coquitlam reminded me somewhat of certain characters created by Voltaire: disillusioned, cynical characters who could see nothing but afflictions, vices, faults and ugliness. I do not wish to devote any more time to a speech so harmful to Canadian unity, towards which all Canadians of good will have strived and especially the right hon. Prime Minister. If the member for Burnaby-Coquitlam thinks he can win votes by saying that the province of Quebec will be the first province to turn communist, he is greatly mistaken, because, to my mind, it is precisely the fear Canadians have of communism that prevents the C.C.F. party from obtaining the success it anticipates in Canadian politics when an appeal is made to the country.
I have respect for the leader of the C.C.F. party (Mr. Coldwell), but I am deeply worried over the opinions expressed by certain members of his party, especially after having heard their speeches. In conclusion I wish only to quote an extract from an article published in the Labour Review, volume 2, No. 3, page 43, under the heading: "Comrades in the C.C.F.", by Herbert Anderson. It proves that our fears are justified in regard to the communist tendencies of certain members of the C.C.F. party. I quote:
Those west-coast CCF people pretty well tipped their hand when they held their annual meeting in Vancouver. To put it bluntly, far too many of them showed up to be communist. A recorded account of their meetings, plus what got into the papers, indicated that between a third and a half of the British Columbia crowd are communist-minded.
The C.C.F. party has not yet disclaimed that article; therefore, I beg Providence to preserve us from the calamity that the C.C.F. party in power would visit upon us.
