speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I expect to have some critical remarks to offer as I proceed. Before proceeding with them I should like to express my appreciation to the government for having announced that the war veterans allowances will be increased during the present session. I am sure I speak for veterans in all parts of Canada when I say this legislation is very much appreciated.
I should also like to thank the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Winters) for the very good news he gave my constituency this afternoon. I mentioned last year that although Mackenzie is a very old constituency it is unable to boast of a single federal public building, and all in one year the minister is proposing to erect three public buildings. In view of the fact that this is our jubilee year in Saskatchewan the people in three communities, Carrot River, Kelvington and Porcupine Plain, will appreciate this very much. Of course the three combined will not cost as much as the national film board buildings which are being erected in the constituency of the hon. member who has just resumed his seat. Those three buildings will cost less than $100,000; nevertheless they will be appreciated.
At this time I am sure I speak for all my colleagues in Saskatchewan when I extend an invitation to all members from all provinces of Canada to visit our province during the recess. Saskatchewan is not the richest province in Canada, but as far as hospitality is concerned we will put out the red carpet for members who can manage to visit us any time during our jubilee year.
The brief which was placed in the hands of members of parliament by the interprovincial farm union council points up a problem which is very real in all parts of Canada. They deal with the crisis which is confronting agriculture. I listened with close interest to the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Stanton), who spoke before the dinner recess and said that members of our group have not discussed the problem which confronts the cheese producers in Ontario. It certainly is not because we are not in sympathy with them, but we have not this industry developed to a very large extent in our constituencies. The problems of the cheese producers are the same problems that the wheat producers and the livestock producers in all provinces of Canada are experiencing.
This brief points out that Canadian agriculture as a whole during the last three years has suffered a most serious setback because of declines in farm product prices, while farmers' costs remained at high levels. They point out that the net farm income in 1951 ran about
$2,188 million. Next year it was down to $1,949 million and the following year to $1,667 million. The estimate for 1954 is $1,200 million, a drop of nearly $1 billion during those three years. They admit that there are places in Canada where agriculture is in quite a healthy position, and there are individual farmers here, there and everywhere who are in a comfortable position; but the whole brief supports the case-and it is well established-that agriculture is facing a major crisis.
In one of his latest bulletins the Minister of Trade and Commerce points out that the farm income is down about 12 per cent for 1954 from the previous year and down about 15 per cent from the all-time high in 1952. The bulletin mentions that the decline in farm income can be attributed in large part to the substantial reduction in returns from the sale of wheat. It is true that the returns from the sale of wheat do bring down the over-all average, but I submit that those of us who live in portions of Canada where our income is from wheat find that this drastic reduction is having most serious consequences.
According to this release, in the province of Saskatchewan the cash income from the sale of farm products in 1953 amounted to $743,352,000 and last year to $465,612,000, a reduction of almost 35 per cent. I need not explain that this is having a most serious effect, and not only in that area where wheat is produced.
The hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Stanton)' mentioned the calamity which has befallen the people of Smiths Falls, which is a few miles from here, involving a very old industry. He said the Frost and Wood Company had been compelled to close its doors and turn a large number of people into the ranks of the unemployed. That is a direct result of the fact that the farmers' income has been reduced so drastically, particularly in western Canada.
The Canadian Federation of Agriculture also analyses what is happening to the farmers' share of the national income in a release dated April, 1954. This gives the share of the national income which went to the farmers in 1926, 1946, 1951, and 1953. In 1926 the farmers' share of the national income was 14-8 per cent; 20 years later it went down to 11 3 per cent, in 1951 it was 12*3 per cent and in 1953, the last year for which the federation have figures available, it was 8-7 per cent. They point out that 13 per cent of the Canadian people are involved in agricultural operations.
One might expect that 13 per cent of the people would receive 13 per cent of the national income. We often pay tribute to the

The Address-Mr. Nicholson farmers as being the salt of the earth, and we recall people in this and other countries getting their start on a farm. If we really mean what we say about the importance of agriculture I think we will readily admit that 8-7 per cent of the national income going to 13 per cent of the people represents a very critical situation indeed.
I received a copy of the report of the royal commission on dominion-provincial relations from the queen's printer the other day. This is a reprint of the material that was prepared by the Rowell-Sirois commission just prior to the outbreak of world war II, and on page 150 of the first volume they present a table showing what happened during the period 1928 to 1933, when conditions such as we are witnessing now developed much more rapidly and all Canada felt the impact. In Saskatchewan the average per capita income fell from $474 to $135, a drop of 72 per cent; in Alberta there was a drop of 61 per cent; in Manitoba 49 per cent, and in Canada as a whole 48 per cent. Other provinces felt the impact as follows: British Columbia, 47 per cent; Prince Edward Island, 45 per cent; Ontario, 44 per cent; Quebec, 44 per cent; New Brunswick, 39 per cent, and Nova Scotia, 36 per cent. The wheat-producing areas were the first to feel the impact and, of course, they felt the consequences much more severely than any other province.
On page 100 of this report there is a very interesting paragraph, and perhaps I should add that this was not written by the present government. It was prepared by the government of which the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) was a cabinet minister some years ago. It states:
The people of Saskatchewan have suffered a reduction in income during the last decade which has probably been unparalleled in peacetime in any other civilized country. Net agricultural income averaging some $200 million a year in the late twenties fell to an actual negative amount in 1931 and 1932, and was only about one-tenth of that average in 1937. Total provincial income (after including federal relief payments in the province) fell in the thirties by more than half, and in the worst years by two-thirds of the 1926-29 annual dollar average.
I am not suggesting that conditions out there are as they were during the thirties, but I am suggesting the drastic reduction in the income of the wheat farmers is having a serious effect on all sectors of our economy, and it is going to require action by the national government to stop this trend and see to it that the agricultural producers in the prairie provinces and in all parts of Canada get their fair share of the national income.


The situation in my own corner of Saskatchewan is more critical than anywhere else in the province, for a variety of factors. We were in the fortunate position of never having had a crop failure during the years of drought when other sections of the west went through year after year without seeing rain. But the last three years have been unparalleled in our history in that we have had so much rain each year that a great many farmers have not had any crop at all as a result of floods and excessive moisture.
I have received reports from ten municipalities in my own constituency; the Minister of Agriculture will be familiar with them. They are Bjorkdale, Buchanan, St. Philips, Sasman, Porcupine, Kelvington, Invermay, Hazel Dell, Livingston, and the L.I.D. office at Hudson Bay, These ten municipalities report to me that at the end of December a year ago they had arrears of taxes totalling $591,096, and at the end of December this year the arrears of taxes were $895,421.
Hon. members will agree, I am sure, that all Canadians wish to pay their taxes first of all, and they are conscious of the vital importance to them of sound municipal government. They are interested in keeping their schools running, in maintaining roads and bridges and other essential services, and therefore an increase in the arrears of taxes in a very productive area in Saskatchewan, to the amount I have mentioned, indicates that the farmers living in that area certainly have not been able to build up bank accounts during prosperous years.
I think the paragraph I read from this publication indicates that there were very good reasons why the farmers in the wheat-producing areas of Canada were unable to build up reserves during the thirties and during the war years when farm commodities were pegged at low prices. The farmers thus were not able to get in as favourable a financial position as many other people in this country.
I also have returns from four of the larger school units in my constituency. These are Tisdale, Canora, Kamsack and Nipawin, which report that they have $789,770 owing to them from municipalities in their area in arrears of taxes, and they in turn owe the banks $429,000 in overdrafts and loans, or an average of over $100,000 per unit at the end of December 1954.
The two sets of figures which I have presented to the house suggest that conditions in that area are certainly very serious. I do not think there is any easy solution for it, but I think we should recognize that the 15 million people in Canada somehow or

other should be able to organize our economy so that those who produce food for our own nation and for our other customers would oe able to get a fair share of the national income so they could have some reserves to put away for bad years, so their arrears of taxes would not pile up as these figures would indicate, and so they would be able to pay their school teachers and give their children all the advantages that are available in other parts of the country. I am not suggesting that there is any easy solution, but I think we can solve it.
During the summer when I was in Europe I took time to visit some of the countries that are facing problems like ours. In Great Britain, at a meeting at the Labour party conference, I was interested to find that one of the best economists there drew their attention to the fact that in Great Britain the farmers are not getting their fair share of the national income, and that if and when labour should form a government again, one of the tasks they must undertake immediately is to see that the farmer in the United Kingdom gets a fairer share of the national income. They said that is not going to be very popular with a large number of trade unions who do not want food prices to increase but, they said, "We want to be fair and we want to make sure that those who are producing food for us get a fair share of the pounds, shillings and pence which are available in Great Britain".
They are embarking on a policy that could easily have fairly serious effects on our economy. They are providing a substantial wheat subsidy. If my figures are correct, something like 65 cents a bushel is being provided as a subsidy to their wheat producers. I pointed out that Canada produces and exports the best wheat in the world. They did not deny that. However, there is a real danger of war and they must give some consideration to what would happen if war broke out and they were entirely dependent on overseas countries, for their foodstuffs, particularly their cereals. Even though it is costing their treasury a good deal of money to increase their production of wheat, they consider that it is in the best interests of the country to provide these subsidies. Something like $6,500,000 is being paid to the 21,000 growers as a result of the policy they are carrying out to encourage the production of their own cereals.
In Sweden I find that once a year the government meets with the representatives of the farmers. They review the general economy of the country and decide on what sort of a deal should be established for the next year for agriculture so the wheat producer, the butter producer and the hog
The Address-Mr. Nicholson producer will all have, for one year, prices which bear a fair relation to the wages and salaries that other people get. The Swedish farmer, when I was there, was being paid $2.28 a bushel for his wheat. This price was some 15 to 20 per cent higher than they would have been paying if they had bought Canadian wheat, but they consider that it is good policy for Sweden to have a healthy, flourishing agricultural industry. The farmers pay something like 75 cents per 230 pounds into a fund to make up for the losses that are involved in connection with the export business. If I remember correctly, they consume about 500,000 tons of wheat in Sweden, but as a result of the policy they have been following since 1947 they have built up quite a substantial surplus. Nearly as much wheat seemed to be on hand as they consume in one year. But the government has been paying $75 million into the fund to support agricultural prices. Sweden has about half the population we have in Canada. Similar support would cost about $150 million in Canada.
In France the price paid to the farmer, as I recall it, was $2.57. I wish we could get international agreement at some time so the metric system could be used all over the world. It is extremely difficult, as you travel about, to figure out the relationship between kilometers and miles and between ounces and grams. The price paid to the French farmer for his wheat was something like $2.57, which seemed to be a reduction of about 15 cents from the price which was paid the previous year. Part of this reduction was as a result of increased productivity in the country. Part of it was as a result of the reduction in prices in France.
There too they take into account the prices the farmer has to pay for his machinery and his fuel oil, and all the other costs he must meet. The prices are reviewed from time to time and they go up or down, depending on a number of these factors. They also are building up quite a large surplus and are reducing the price with a view to discouraging the building up of such a large surplus.
They also have a policy there-I am not sure that it is too sound-of paying a higher price to smaller operators. Those who deliver quintals-I have forgotten what the relationship is between quintals and bushels-are paid according to the number they deliver. If they deliver between 1 to 25 quintals, the net price to the farmer is 3,570 francs. One who is selling from 100 to 200 gets a price of 3,440 francs. If you are selling over 1,000, your price is down to 3,315 francs. This policy has been worked out, no doubt, to encourage the smaller farmers in France to
656	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Nicholson keep up their production. The assumption is that the larger operators are able to cut down their operating costs.
In West Germany there was an agricultural policy that was extremely favourable to the farmers. The wheat farmer had a price of about $2.63 to $2.73 a bushel. The prices for barley were much higher than those in Canada. Barley prices were from $1.76 to $2.20, and $1 to $1.26 for oats. In Germany they have another policy-one that we have been trying to persuade the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Agriculture to adopt-to encourage farm storage. For wheat there is a payment of about 12-6 cents per bushel extra to the farmer on condition that he keeps his grain on his farm rather than filling up the elevator space, and about 11-7 cents for rye.
I do not wish to suggest, Mr. Speaker, that I should like to live in any of these countries I have mentioned, or that I should like to farm in them. I have said repeatedly that while I was away I did not see any country that I liked as well as Canada and that farming, as I saw it in these European countries, does not appear to me to be as attractive as does farming in Saskatchewan, even with the low prices we are getting and the other problems that we want to solve at some time. But I think it is significant that in these countries I have mentioned they are devoting a great deal of thought and effort to increasing the production of foodstuffs as part of an over-all national policy.
I am aware of the problem we might have on our hands here if the Minister of Agriculture and the Minister of Trade and Commerce guaranteed prices, such as we did in the past. Canada has a tremendous capacity to produce agricultural products. In this world in which we live, with all its tensions,
I think we should recognize that producing food is one activity that should be encouraged and that Canada should go all out first of all to see that every Canadian citizen is able to obtain maximum quantities of food.
I received a letter today from the old age pensioners in British Columbia containing a table showing the increase in the cost of foods over a period of years, and they suggest that the pension should be increased. I cannot think of any good reason why, with this large surplus of butter, every old age pensioner in Canada should not have the benefit of the suggestion made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. In the United States they worked out a stamp plan some years ago when they had these problems. Everybody in a certain category got stamps entitling them to butter, fruits and a wide variety of surplus products they had at that time in the United States.

speechtext:
My first remarks, Mr. Speaker, will be to offer my congratulations to the mover (Mr. Leduc) and seconder (Mr. Carrick) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I would say that both discharged their task in a manner that promises well for their future as members of this house.
I believe that the speech from the throne justifies us in feeling that this session will be a very fruitful one. I particularly underline certain measures which will help to alleviate the burden now on the shoulders of a large number of Canadians who are totally or partly dependent upon public assistance in solving their personal and family problems. Every member of this house learned with great satisfaction of the decision taken by the government to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act to provide an increase in the duration and scale of supplementary benefits, as well as other amendments intended to make unemployment insurance of greater benefit to the unemployed.
The National Housing Act of 1954, adopted during the last session, will be broadened to enable landlords to obtain loans for home improvements. I hope this will pave the way for a full rural loan measure, similar to that existing in some provinces, for farm owners. At this point I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll) upon his timely suggestion that the national housing scheme be amended to give home owners the same protection as that given to the lending institutions. This would be provided by means of equity insurance, at a premium the prospective owner could pay, to protect him against the loss of his initial investment.
After a splendid exposition of the many reasons militating in favour of his suggestion, and the procedure which could be followed

The Address-Mr. Dupuis if it were carried out, our learned colleague went on to say at page 110 of Hansard for January 12:
I believe it is the duty of the government, which is encouraging him to invest his all in a national housing home, to offer him a measure of protection. At the present time the government is protecting lending institutions by insuring the amount of the mortgage. With that I am in full accord and agreement. You can believe me that the lending institution, with its funds spread over thousands of investments, and secured in each case by property, is far less in need of protection than the national housing owner, who has all his eggs in one basket.
At the present time, and quite properly, the government protects the national housing mortgagee, and it is my view that it should protect the national housing owner, at least to the extent of his initial down payment. Every owner is far more vulnerable than the lending institution. No matter what happens, the lending institution cannot lose. In the event of a foreclosure it will look first to the property, and then to the government for repayment. But the owner may very well be wiped out.
I sincerely hope the government will give consideration to this timely suggestion. This will be another opportunity to show that this party has always been concerned with seeing that the small owners get the security to which they are justly entitled.
The government is to be praised also for increasing the basic rate, as well as the ceiling on permissible income, of the recipients of war veterans allowances. These veterans already derive benefit from the generous War Veterans Allowance Act. Other changes will be proposed to the national defence and defence services acts. I welcome also the fact that consideration is being given to the request to lower the eligible age for blind pensions, and to raise the income ceilings for these unfortunate people. Fishermen ought to be equally happy to learn of the decision taken by this government which will enable them to obtain loans on a similar basis as that provided in the Farm Improvement Loans Act.
The government, having taken into account the regional and seasonal unemployment which now exists, and which we all deplore, is endeavouring to help this situation by accelerating public construction projects already approved and assuring financial provision for the construction programs of various departments and agencies on an enlarged scale. The proposed amendment to the Railway Act to provide for the elimination of level crossings must not be overlooked. This might help to eliminate tragic accidents and accelerate traffic at these points.
These good measures have been the objects of laudable comments not only by members on this side of the house but also by the

Acting Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Rowe) and some of his followers, as well as other members sitting on the opposite side of the house. According to the Conservative party's spokesman, many of his followers have reason to be thankful to the government for the realization of projects or measures they had advocated in the past.
The Acting Leader of the Opposition said the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks) would certainly have read the speech from the throne with a little chuckle to himself and would be glad that at last the government had heeded his pleas on behalf of the war veterans. He went on to say that the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) also had reason for being happy because of the blasting, in the near future, of Ripple Rock, an improvement that hon. member has ardently advocated.
The hon. member for Queens (Mr. MacLean), still according to the Acting Leader of the Opposition, would also be justified in rejoicing when he heard that steady progress was being made toward the inauguration of the new ferry service between Prince Edward Island and the mainland of Nova Scotia, and that the project would be undertaken this year. Another observation by the acting leader was to the effect that the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mrs. Fairclough), who is very moderate in distributing compliments to the government, along with her colleague the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Starr), should be delighted to note that supplementary benefits would be extended to the unemployed during the winter months.
Of course the acting leader intentionally failed to mention the efforts made by members on this side of the house in favour of the measures now lauded by the government antagonists. Nevertheless, we of this party are particularly proud to receive these testimonies, and to use the words of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) I will say: "although it is somewhat of an exaggeration to suggest that anything of which we are supposed to be boasting as an achievement is due to pressure put upon us by suggestions from the other side of the house, nevertheless we will be happy to give serious consideration to any constructive suggestion, whatever its source. The genuine welfare of the country is, or should be, of more concern to all of us". These words illustrate the sense of duty of our leader. On all occasions he has manifested his firm determination to serve the best interests of our country in a non-partisan manner.
Now let us study the amendment moved by the Acting Leader of the Opposition and

seconded by the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker). It reads as follows:
We regret that Your Excellency's advisers have failed to take or to recommend the necessary measures:	(a) to retain and expand Canada's
markets abroad for our production, particularly of wheat and other products; (b) to solve the urgent problem of unemployment; (c) to relieve Canadian taxpayers from the burden of excessive taxation and thereby enable Canadian producers to lower their cost of production and to meet increasing competition; (d) to eliminate waste and extravagance in government and improve its efficiency; (e) to facilitate and encourage the processing of our natural resources in Canada, and thereby increase opportunities and employment for Canadians; (f) in co-operation with the provinces to develop an effective contributory plan which will assure that every Canadian will have adequate hospital and medical services.
As to the first paragraph, I leave it to those who are better acquainted with the problems of international markets to supply the information, which in my opinion will show the efforts made by this government to retain the advantages deriving from our commercial relations with other countries, especially with the commonwealth nations. I thought representatives of the opposition would offer suggestions to improve our situation in this connection. If they have not found a better solution than this government has, they ought to be rather bashful about inserting such a paragraph in the amendment.
On the other hand, if members of the opposition have in mind ways of bettering present conditions, they should let us hear them. It is their duty to do so. They may have the intention of taking adequate steps to blast their way into the overseas or the United States or South American and other markets, as the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett said he would but was unable or did not have the ability to carry out. At all events let them tell us how they would tackle and solve this problem.
The Acting Leader of the Opposition must know a lot about blasting into the international markets, as he was a member of the government at that time. In the meantime I prefer to place my confidence in the Minister of Trade and Commerce, who is well aware of the situation and whose competence is a safeguard that no opportunity will be neglected in order to find the best possible solution to this problem, with all the unexpected changes to which it is subject.
The second paragraph of the amendment states that the government has failed to take necessary measures to solve the urgent problem of unemployment. All of us in this house deplore that unemployment exists at any time of the year, especially in the wintertime. As 1 have said previously, this
The Address-Mr. Dupuis government has taken the necessary steps to help those who are affected by unemployment by extending the period and increasing the rate of the allowances during the winter months, and also by making large appropriations for public works. I represent a constituency whose population is composed almost entirely of workingmen. Anything done to increase the possibilities of employment will receive my approval. I shall discuss this matter at greater length on another occasion.
Let me refer now to paragraph (c) of the amendment, in which the opposition blames the government for not relieving Canadian taxpayers from the burden of excessive taxation, thereby enabling Canadian producers to lower their cost of production and meet increasing competition. Like every other citizen I would like to see a reduction in the heavy taxes we are paying. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) seems to be of the same opinion. He made a declaration recently, although he did not commit himself. Let us hope that we can expect a move in that direction. Like everyone else I am anxious to hear the next budget speech.
I am not blaming my hon. friends of the opposition for making such a popular suggestion, but I would like them to be a little more logical. On the one hand members of all the opposition parties demand the lowering of taxes and, on the other hand, they are asking constantly for higher expenditures in connection with welfare allowances and public works.
I favour the execution of public works on a large scale, especially in seasons when unemployment is high, but I think all will agree with me when 1 say that public works after all are disguised taxes because the money required is taken from revenue, from the money the government has to dispose of, which consists almost entirely of funds raised through direct taxation on the individual.
As far as increasing welfare allowances is concerned, I shall later analyse what has been done in this connection by the party which has received the support of the people for a longer period of time than any other party since confederation.
There is one timely suggestion in the amendment which in my opinion should be given further consideration by the government. I refer to the paragraph which reads: To facilitate and encourage the processing of our natural resources in Canada.
I have on several occasions, in this house and elsewhere, expressed my opinion on this matter. A larger proportion of our national resources can be processed here. I know this

The Address-Mr. Dupuis government has encouraged this policy, as have some of the provinces, but there is room for greater improvement in this regard.
Paragraph (f) of the amendment relates to the provision of adequate hospital and medical services. Everyone knows that such services are mainly the responsibility of the provinces. However, let us see what this government has done in the sphere of social assistance during the period from 1948 to 1953, leaving aside the achievements of other Liberal governments in this connection. During that period of time subventions or grants paid to the provinces by the federal government amounted to $167,407,831 for crippled children, professional training, hospital construction, venereal disease treatment, mental hygiene, tuberculosis and cancer control.

(Text):
A total of $94 million was paid during the same period to provinces which had spent an equal amount under the terms of the agreement between the federal government and the provinces.
I might also mention other forms of subsidies or contributions made by the federal government to the provinces for such purposes as the training of health workers, the training of nurses, the training of nursing assistants, mental health, and the employment of health workers. To this we must also add the salaries paid to the persons trained or undergoing training under the national health program, such as physicians, dentists, nurses, sanitation personnel, technicians, statisticians, and many others specialized or specializing in various other fields of public health. The number of those on the payroll totalled 4,947 during the period 1948 to 1953.
We have learned with great satisfaction from the report issued by the department of health and welfare that the federal government will offer additional financial aid to the provinces to help create (a) better health care for the disabled; (b) better health care for mothers and children; (c) better facilities and services to help doctors diagnose their patients' illnesses. The amount to be voted for that purpose is $42,000,000 for the next five years. These figures can be obtained because they are published by the department. All this does not take into account other sums spent by the Department of National Health and Welfare for special studies and research in laboratories, in the food inspection division and in many other items.
This is proof that the federal government, contrary to what the opposition claims, has accomplished a great deal in assuring adequate medical services. I understand that the plan for national health insurance is still being considered, and that negotiations are under way between the federal and provincial authorities. I hope they will lead to a mutual understanding between the interested governments which will be to the advantage of the people, especially the working class who cannot afford to meet the prohibitive cost of hospitalization. Incidentally I will say that in Montreal last year $695,000 was given to the neurological institute. That shows that a lot has been done to provide adequate medical services.

Before concluding my remarks on this subject I wish to draw the attention of my colleagues to the fact that out of the $167 million which was allotted to them during the period 1948-53, the provinces have used only some $94 million. It is up to each province to make full use of the federal contributions to expand hospital accommodation and medical services. Much more can be accomplished in that direction; and referring to the province of Quebec only I will say that there is a very great need for more hospital space, especially for those afflicted with mental illnesses. What more do our friends opposite need to prove that adequate hospital and medical services are receiving the attention of this government?

I do not have to change sides to be right. I am right on both sides. Must I deduce from the words of the member for Quebec West that he would be talking differently if he were on this side? Unless one is as blind as a bat he must recognize the splendid work accomplished by this government in the sphere of public health. I wish to seize the present opportunity to congratulate the Minister of National Health and Welfare, who at all times has proven his ardent desire to ensure the best health and welfare conditions for our citizens. He has accomplished a wonderful task for which the people of Canada are grateful; that is, excluding the opposition members.
Now let us see what else has been done in the last 20 years under different Liberal governments in the field of public welfare, leaving aside the unemployment insurance scheme which has been so profitable to the workers of this country. In 1927 old age pensions were paid at the rate of $20 a month to people 70 years of age and over. The rate was raised to $25 a month in 1943 and the means test scale broadened. The allowance was again raised to $30 a month in 1947, and to $40 in 1949. This was a Liberal measure enacted by a Liberal government. In 1952 the age at which a person was entitled to old age pension was reduced to 65, and old age security and old age assistance guaranteed to every citizen 70 years of age and over. In the first case the means test scale was maintained. Let us bear in mind that not only have the aged people been given assistance at an earlier age than that requested when this measure was first put into force, but the monthly allowances have been doubled since this party has been in power. That is not such a bad record.
It was in 1945 that the government, under a Liberal administration, instituted family
The Address-Mr. Dupuis allowances entirely at the cost of the federal government. I am sure nobody ever thought that $5 or $6 a month was enough to maintain a child. The intention of the sponsors of such a good social measure was to alleviate the burden entailed in bringing up a family. Some are asking to double this allowance. I certainly favour this suggestion, although it would mean an extra expenditure of $400 million. Incidentally, the number of families in receipt of this allowance at the present time is around two million, representing five million children. I hope when the situation created by the menace of war disappears, which necessitates the spending of huge sums to assure our national safety, more generous allowances in all spheres of social security or welfare will be provided by this government.
As I just said, the whole cost of family allowances is borne by the federal government. I realize that doubling them would be a great help to a large number of fathers and mothers. Even $10 a month will not be enough, mind you-and every member in this house knows that as well as I do-to look after the necessities of life and the education of a child. However, I would favour such an increase. I do not want to pass the buck to someone else, as we commonly say, but I sincerely submit that the different provinces should make it their duty to allocate to their residents a monthly allowance at the same rate as that granted by the federal government.
My friends of the Social Credit party in my province have launched a wide campaign in favour of the doubling of family allowances. I hope they succeed. Mr. Speaker, in taking part in this debate, after it has gone on for so many days and after so many speeches have been made, I shall endeavour not to be guilty of too much repetition. After listening to the previous speaker, may I say that if the committee on


procedure of this house can cut the length of speeches to 30 minutes, I think it would meet the desires of most hon. members.
The speech from the throne is a document that is prepared by the government and is handed to the Governor General to read at the opening of parliament. At this time I want to congratulate the two new members who moved and seconded the address in reply for the effort they put into the preparation of their speeches. From what I have learned from reading the speech from the throne and from listening to the previous speeches, this document is a fairly calm one. In it there is nothing about securing trade or markets for Canadian farm products. There is not even a reference to the pilgrimage to Washington of the three cabinet ministers a few weeks ago for the purpose of securing trade. They must have come back empty-handed because this government is so boastful about things they do that, if they had received any extra trade agreements or things of that sort, we certainly would have heard about it long before now. In the speech from the throne there is not even a reference to that pilgrimage to Washington.
The employment situation is treated as though it were seasonal and unimportant. I think it was the Minister of Trade and Commerce who said it was regional. It is regional all right, because it has permeated every region and every part of Canada. Then someone said that the 600,000 unemployed were an unimportant matter. It may be unimportant to this government, especially to the cabinet, but it certainly is not unimportant to the people of Canada, especially those who are out of work. When 600,000 are out of work it means 600,000 families who are unhappy at this time.
We have had the promise of public works projects, but no indication is given as to what they are or how much is involved. I may be of an unduly suspicious nature, but I suspect that too much has been made of them already and that not half the projects we anticipate will actually be undertaken. There are, however, two proposed matters of legislation that are welcomed. One is the increase in the war veterans allowance, for which the Conservative party has fought for years. The other is the proposed reduction in the qualification age for blind pensions. That is something that is all to the good.
I also recall a recent speech by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) advising the people of Canada to be calm. Calmness has a place, but it is asking much of Canadians to be calm in the face of unemployment which is steadily

rising, and to be calm with the continuing loss of export markets. Incidentally, the raising of unemployment insurance payments and the granting of winter bonuses will be appreciated by the people who are out of work, and will tend to alleviate but will not solve the problem of unemployment.
Are the labour forces to be calm in the face of increasing unemployment? Are Canadians to be calm in the face of being subjected to super-heavy taxation which is far above that which is needed to maintain our defences and other branches of government, and which bears so heavily on the lower income families? Are Canadians to be calm when they know that super-taxation has done its part to place prohibitive price tags on the goods they have to buy and on products for which markets have to be found abroad? Shall Canadians be calm when they know that corporate taxation at present super-high rates is killing the goose that lays the golden egg? Without fair profits there cannot be jobs. That statement applies to government-owned industries as well as to private business, as has been proven by the the province of Saskatchewan's experiment in socialist enterprise.
All of us will welcome the expected reductions in taxation this session, although no reference is made thereto in the speech from the throne. This is a course the Progressive Conservative party has advocated for years, but these reductions are several years too late. What of the farmers and other primary producers who are caught in a vise-like squeeze between falling prices for farm products and rising costs of the things they have to buy? Are they to be calm? What of the pensioners whose pensions have been greatly devalued by the cost of living? Are they to be calm? These are but a few of the problems affecting Canada's economy at the present time.
A few days ago the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) said he had more amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act to bring before this house. As I said before, everybody appreciates the amendment that was recently passed, but we would welcome other amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act. I do not see why he is waiting. Why does he not bring them in now instead of telling us that he is going to do so later on in the session? If it is going to be for the benefit of the workers, and if it is going to help the unemployment situation, they should be introduced now. The people need them now.
Then as to the matter of unemployment insurance benefits, even with the benefits that have been added for the winter months these benefits are running out fast in many places. What happens when the benefits run out? You know what happens. The people line up at the relief desks in the municipali-
The Address-Mr. Hodgson ties. Who pays the relief? The municipality, to be sure. Does this government help the municipality to pay its relief costs? Not one iota. Is unemployment in Canada the responsibility of this government? Why, certainly it is. Everyone knows it is the responsibility of the federal government. Therefore the federal government should dig down into its pocket and come to the aid of the municipalities in paying their relief costs.
In my own constituency 30 per cent of the labouring men are out of work. In the northern half of my constituency 50 per cent of the men are out of work. The reason is that it is a tourist and lumbering district, and when the tourists go in the fall there is nothing for the people to lean upon except the lumbering industry. Many workmen from other parts of Canada drift into the Hali-burton area looking for work in the winter months. They have drifted there this year, but there has been no work for them. The only thing they have done is to increase the number on relief. There are more lining up for relief every day at the municipal offices.
What has happened to the economy of the lumbering industry in Canada? I can tell you. We have lost the British market. When Canada lost the British market for lumber, British Columbia lumber started to come into Ontario. British Columbia lumber producers cut the price and competed with our producers on the 8, 10, 12, 14 and 16 foot lengths that we produce in Ontario. In British Columbia their lumber is produced in longer lengths, and when their yards are piled full with short lengths they become a drug on the market and they can afford to ship them to Ontario and undersell us so far as price is concerned.
There must be something more than that behind the situation. I saw in a newspaper a few days ago that New Zealand has recruited 100 Canadian lumberjacks to work in that country. The government of New Zealand is considering coming to Canada to get more forest labourers to go to their [DOT]country to work in their lumber industry. How is it that they can manage to produce lumber in New Zealand? Their market must be the same market as ours. That is the situation at the present time so far as my riding is concerned. We cannot sell any lumber.
There is one other point about the unemployment situation that I think I should mention, and it has to do with the Canadian National Railways. The Belleville division is in my riding, and the Canadian National Railways have sent out an order laying off 60 section crew men in that division. That cuts that labour force right in two. You had an average of four men to a section taking

The Address-Mr. Hodgson care of and maintaining 7 miles of track and now there will be four men taking care of 17 miles. The order is to become effective on the 1st of February.
Snow removal costs have been twice as great this year as in any of the last ten years. The idea of cutting the number of section-men is not new. The present set-up in the Belleville division has been in operation for 30 years to my knowledge. The same crews have been taking care of the same mileage, maintaining the same number of miles of track. But now the C.N.R. has seen fit to knock off 60 men and cut the number right in two. Hours of labour are shorter now than they were 15 years ago. Men do not do as much hard work as they used to, but the C.N.R. is going to ask these men to do twice as much work with half as many men.
It appears to the employees that this move is simply retaliation by the C.N.R. on account of the fringe benefits awarded the men by Mr. Justice Sloan in the arbitration of a few months ago. In 1951 the Canadian National Railways came forward with the very same program at about the same time of year. I spoke in the house on the matter at the time. The order went out, but for some reason or other it was not put into effect; the situation was left unchanged and has remained that way up until the present time. In 1951 there were 6 roadmasters on the Belleville division and today they have 21. There are to be fewer sectionmen with more miles to cover and there is more snow to remove, but there are three times as many roadmasters. I think certain types of work on the C.N.R. could stand to be investigated, because it seems to me that the railway is overloaded with officials from top to bottom.
Men are being moved all over the system. Men with 40 years of service are affected and are going to be moved about from one part of the country to another if they wish to hold their jobs. The younger men of course are the ones who will be laid off. The C.N.R. has 50 per cent more officials than the C.P.R., on the basis of the number of labouring men. No wonder the Canadian National comes back to parliament every year and wants more money to operate the road. It is no fault of the men. There are just as good men on the Canadian National as there are on the Canadian Pacific or any other railroad on the North American continent. It is a question of too much officialdom and too high salaries in the top brackets of officials.
Some few years ago I put a question on the order paper in an endeavour to find out what were the salaries of some of the top men of the C.N.R., but that question was never answered. I think I shall try again


this year. It may only be a try, but sometimes it is worth it.
I should like to do a little advertising of my own riding. Several things are happening there that I hope will produce a lot of work and be of value to our country. I refer to the discovery of uranium. It is not a new find. Dr. Hugh Spence, the head of the metallurgical service of the department in Ottawa, wrote an article on it in 1932. It was fresh in the minds of the government at that time. Plenty of people asked the government to do something about it, but instead the government spent a billion dollars at Eldorado when there was uranium at the back door of their Chalk River plant.

Eastern Canada
1.	The Minister of Agriculture is authorized to pay freight assistance on:
(a)	Western wheat, oats, barley, rye, wheat bran, wheat shorts, wheat middlings, No. 1 feed screenings and No. 2 feed screenings, shipped or transported by rail or boat from Port Arthur, Fort William or Armstrong, Ontario, to destinations in Canada east thereof and distributed for use exclusively as feed in Canada for Canadian livestock or poultry;
(b)	Wheat bran, wheat shorts and wheat middlings milled in western Canada, or milled in eastern Canada from western wheat shipped or transported from Port Arthur, Fort William or Armstrong, Ontario, to port elevators or flour mills in Canada east thereof when such bran, shorts, or middlings are distributed from the manufacturing mill for use exclusively as feed in Canada for Canadian livestock or poultry.
2.	The payment of freight assistance authorized pursuant to section 1 shall be as follows:
(a)	On all rail shipments to destinations in northern Ontario the payment shall be the actual carlot rail freight charges but not exceeding $4.50 per ton;
(b)	On all shipments to destinations in Ontario, except northern Ontario, the payment shall be $4.50 per ton;
(c)	On all shipments to destinations, other than those in Ontario, the payment shall be $4.50 per ton if the destination is within the Montreal freight rate zone and $4.50 per ton plus the remainder of the through carlot rail freight rate in excess of the Montreal freight rate zone rate if the destination is beyond the Montreal freight rate zone provided that such destination has a through carlot rail freight rate below 80 cents per hundredweight; if the destination of the shipment has a through carlot rail freight rate of 80 cents per hundredweight or higher the payment shall be $6.00 per ton plus the remainder of the through carlot rail freight rate in excess of the Montreal freight rate zone rate;
(d)	The rates of payment under paragraph
(c)	shall not be increased while this order is in effect irrespective of any

increase in all rail through carlot rail freight rates which would result in the balance of such rate over the Montreal freight rate zone rate being higher than it is at the time this order becomes effective.
British Columbia
3.	The Minister of Agriculture is authorized to pay freight assistance on:
(a)	Western wheat, oats, barley, rye, corn, No. 1 feed screenings and No. 2 feed screenings, wheat bran, wheat shorts and wheat middlings, shipped from points of origin in the provinces of Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba and in that part of British Columbia known as the Peace river district, to destinations in British Columbia and distributed for use exclusively as feed in British Columbia for Canadian livestock or poultry;
(b)	Wheat bran, wheat shorts and wheat middlings milled in British Columbia from western wheat, shipped from points of origin as designated in paragraph (a), and distributed as designated in paragraph (a).
4.	The payment of freight assistance authorized pursuant to section 3 shall be $5.00 per ton less than the carlot short line rail freight charges from Calgary or Edmonton or the point of origin in Alberta, whichever is the lowest, to destinations in British Columbia, and to pay the coastal water carlot shipping charges from any coastal point in British Columbia to any other coastal point therein but not exceeding the balance of the through rail carlot freight rate if the said coastal point is served by rail, provided that if the carlot rail freight rates are increased while this order is in effect the unpaid portion of the charges shall be increased by an amount equal to the increase in the said rail freight rates.
General
5.	On all grains and feeds shipped and distributed in accordance with the provisions of this order, evidence satisfactory to the minister must be produced to show that the sale price to consumers of such products has been reduced by and takes into account the payment of freight assistance as herein prescribed.
Monday, January 31, 1955
